entries.narration: This course builds one data platform on Azure, for one bank, to answer one question. The bank is Woodgrove Bank, and it finances trade. When an importer buys goods from a supplier abroad, the supplier will not ship on trust, so the bank issues a letter of credit: a promise to pay the supplier once the shipping documents arrive. The importer repays the bank later. Until it does, the bank is owed money, and that is the question: how much could the bank lose, and to whom? Start on the left. Wide World Importers, in the U K, is a counterparty: a company that owes the bank. It has two letters of credit open, for three million and two million dollars, and it has just asked for a third, L C two oh four one, for two million more. Wide World Logistics, in Singapore, has one for two and a half million. Both companies belong to Wide World Group. If one of them fails, the other often fails with it, so the bank adds them up at the group, and it sets its limit at the group: ten million dollars. Now the middle. Open deals come to seven and a half million; the new one makes nine and a half. That is the gross exposure. Against it the bank holds collateral: half a million in cash, counted in full, and a warehouse of goods worth a million, counted at only six hundred thousand, because goods may sell for less in a hurry. That forty percent cut is the haircut. Nine and a half, less one point one, leaves a net exposure of eight point four million. It is inside the ten million limit, with one point six to spare. Underneath, one more test. The regulator wants every group whose exposure is above ten percent of the bank's own money, its capital. Woodgrove's capital is eighty million, so the line is eight million, and Wide World, at eight point four, goes on the large exposures report. On the right are the ten words this needs, and they are the only finance in the course. Beneath them is why one answer is never enough. A new deal raises exposure and a repayment lowers it. Prices and currency rates change what the collateral is worth, even while nobody is booking anything. And when one group buys a company, that company's deals move under the buyer's limit. So the answer has to be computed again every day, and every number here will be computed by the platform we build. Next, how the bank answers this question today.

Answering the risk question for one group took four numbers. Answering it for every group, every morning, takes five systems, and they do not talk to each other. On the left is where the numbers live. TradeBook is the bank's booking system, a database in the bank's own data centre, and it holds every deal. The hierarchy file says which company belongs to which group, and it arrives at six in the evening. The limits extract carries each group's limit at half past six. The collateral file, with what is held and its haircuts, lands at seven. And the market feed sends currency rates and prices all day, because a warehouse of goods priced in euros is worth a different number of dollars every hour. Today an analyst copies all of it into one spreadsheet, on one laptop, and builds the large exposures report from it. The report is due at seven in the morning. The table in the middle is a typical morning, and its times are illustrative. Exporting yesterday's deals starts at six. Matching them to groups takes until twenty past seven, collateral and haircuts until five to eight, currencies and limits until quarter past, and checking the result by eye until half past eight. The report goes out ninety minutes late. The list beneath it is what goes wrong. The numbers are a day old before anyone reads them. A company that changed owner last week is still counted in its old group, so a breach can hide. Nobody can re-run the morning and get the same answer twice. And when the analyst is ill, there is no report at all. The last list is the brief for the rest of this course. The platform must land every source, every day, in one place. It must keep the data inside the U K and inside the bank's network. It must compute exposure overnight and keep it fresh through the day. And it must publish by seven: an A P I for the risk team, alerts for credit officers, and a report that nobody can change once it is filed. Next, why renting computers suits a job like this one.

A risk platform is not busy all day. It is very busy for a short time, and nearly idle the rest. The plot on the left is the platform's day, and it stays the same for the whole course. From midnight to two in the morning, the overnight run computes exposure for every group, and it needs sixteen workers to finish in time. From eight in the morning to six in the evening, an intraday refresh recomputes exposure as prices move, and two workers are enough. The rest of the day there is nothing to compute. The dashed line is what owning means. If the bank buys machines, it must buy for the busiest hour, so it owns sixteen, all day. The tables on the right put numbers on it. Sixteen machines for twenty four hours is three hundred and eighty four worker hours of capacity a day. The work uses fifty two of them: thirty two in the night and twenty during the day. The machines are busy fourteen percent of the time, and they cost the same idle as busy. Renting changes the unit. With a cloud provider, the bank pays for each worker for the hours it runs. At a rate of twenty cents a worker hour, which is a hypothetical rate used only for comparison, fifty two hours cost ten dollars forty a day. The same capacity held all day would cost seventy six dollars eighty. The list underneath says what else changes. Capacity arrives in minutes, not after a purchase order and a delivery. Stopped capacity stops costing, mostly; the next course shows what keeps charging when nothing runs. The night can use sixteen workers and the day two, from the same account. And the ceiling is no longer what was bought, but a quota, a number Azure sets per subscription that the bank can ask to raise. None of this is free: someone still has to decide how many workers, when, and who may start them. That is what the rest of the course builds. Next, how much of the work Azure can take on beyond renting machines.

Renting machines is only the first step. Azure will also run the software on them, and every service draws the line between the bank's work and Microsoft's in a different place. Read the row from left to right. A server the bank owns, in its own data centre, is all the bank's: the building, the power, the hardware, the operating system, every piece of software and every patch. A virtual machine on Azure, a V M, takes the building and the hardware away; Microsoft runs those and the hypervisor that keeps one customer's machines apart from another's. The bank still installs and patches the operating system and everything on it. This is called infrastructure as a service, and the platform will use one for its integration runtime, the program that reaches into the bank's data centre. One step right is Azure Database for PostgreSQL, flexible server. Now Microsoft installs the database engine, patches it and the operating system in a maintenance window the bank may choose, takes the backups and handles failover. The bank decides the size, designs the tables and owns the data. This is platform as a service. Data Factory is platform as a service too: the bank writes pipelines and schedules and keeps the secrets they connect with, and Microsoft runs the service and scales the copying. At the far right is Power B I, software as a service: the bank only builds reports and decides who sees them. The table below names the trade. Moving right, the bank does fewer jobs, but has less control over versions, operating system access and tuning. It lives inside the service's limits, which Microsoft documents as quotas. And it pays closer to use: per hour, per gigabyte, per pipeline run. The list on the right says where the platform uses each: a V M for the integration runtime and Data Factory for the batches in course eight, PostgreSQL for the risk mart in course eleven, and Power B I for the analysts in course twelve. Next, the one question that every one of these services raises: who is responsible for its security?

Once part of the system belongs to Microsoft and part to the bank, every security job needs an owner. Microsoft calls this the shared responsibility model. On the left are the two ends of it. Some jobs are always Microsoft's, whatever the service: the datacentres and the people guarding them, the hosts and their disks, the physical network, the hypervisor, the software inside each managed service, and the Regions and zones themselves. Some jobs are always the bank's, also whatever the service: its data and how it is labelled, the accounts and identities that sign in, the laptops they sign in from, who may reach what, the network rules, and every setting the bank chooses. Microsoft's own guidance names three of these as never transferring to the provider: information and data, devices, and accounts and identities. The table on the right shows how the middle moves. Physical hardware is Microsoft's everywhere. The operating system is the bank's on a V M and Microsoft's on PostgreSQL. On Azure Databricks, the cluster's runtime image is built and patched by Databricks, and the bank chooses which version to run and restarts its clusters onto a new one, as the note beneath says. Code and jobs are the bank's on every service that runs them. And the last three rows never move: network rules, who may use the service, and the data with its encryption keys belong to the bank on every column, including plain storage. The list at the bottom turns the table into incidents. A host failing under a V M is Microsoft's problem, and it restarts the machine elsewhere. A lake that accepts traffic from the internet is the bank's, because Azure did exactly what it was configured to do. An integration V M that misses a security patch is the bank's. A PostgreSQL engine patch is Microsoft's, applied in the window the bank set. Most cloud security failures sit in the bank's half, and most of this course is about doing that half well. Next, the whole platform we are going to build.

Here is the platform the course builds, finished, on one map. Every frame that shows the map from now on shows this same picture, in the same place, so you always know where you are. Data flows down. At the top are the bank's own systems, which exist before Azure is involved: TradeBook, the daily files and the market feed. To their right is the private network that carries their data into Azure: an ExpressRoute circuit from the bank's data centre, a virtual network, and private endpoints, so no service has to face the internet. Below is the platform itself, in the U K South Region, in a production subscription. The ingest row brings data in: an integration runtime and Data Factory for the batches, Event Grid to notice a file arriving, Event Hubs for the market feed and Service Bus for the steps of each deal. The next row stores and computes: the lake, Databricks, which transforms the data overnight, and a container of locked reports; beside it, the stores that serve results: a PostgreSQL risk mart, a Cosmos D B lookup by group and a cache. The publish row is everything the risk team touches: the exposure A P I, A P I Management in front of it, a function that raises breach alerts, a workflow that escalates them, a job that files the report, and Power B I. At the bottom are the readers: Front Door for the bank's office in Singapore, the risk team and the regulator. The column on the right wraps everything: Entra I D and role-based access, managed identities, Policy, Key Vault, Bicep and the pipeline that deploys it, Monitor, Defender, Backup and cost. On the right of the frame is the course as the order we build it in, from a first storage container in course three to a priced and reviewed design in course fourteen. Each course adds the parts the platform needs next. A grey outline on the map is a part not built yet, and an alternative is always drawn beside the map, never inside it. The table at the bottom names the four kinds of frame you will see: this map; the map beside a command and its output; an editor, with one file of the project run in a terminal beneath it; and a concept frame, for an idea with no command at all. The Databricks box is built in this course from the Azure side; what runs inside it is taught in the Databricks course. Next, how Azure itself receives and runs a request.

Before the platform has anything in it, it needs a place, and Azure's places are nested boundaries, each one containing a different kind of failure. On the left is the United Kingdom, which Azure calls a geography. Inside it are two Regions. U K South, in London, is where the platform will run. It has three availability zones: separate datacentres, or groups of them, each with its own power, cooling and network, close enough to each other for fast replication. U K West, in Cardiff, has no availability zones at all. The two Regions are a region pair, which Microsoft uses for recovery: some services can copy data from one to the other, and Microsoft staggers planned updates across a pair. The first table names what each boundary contains. A host is one machine; if it fails, a virtual machine restarts on another. A zone contains the loss of a datacentre. A Region contains everything inside it, so only something outside the Region survives a regional disaster. And a geography is about law, not failure: keeping both Regions in the U K keeps the bank's data in the U K. The second table plays out zone two being lost, drawn in red on the left. The lake, stored with zone-redundant storage, keeps three copies across the zones and keeps serving. The risk mart, with zone-redundant high availability, fails over to its standby in another zone and carries on after a short pause. One integration machine in zone two simply stops; two of them, in zones one and three, keep working. That is the whole idea of zones: a design has to spread itself across them, or they protect nothing. The last list names what these are not. Zone numbers are logical, per subscription, so your zone one may be a different building from someone else's. A region pair is for recovery, not for spreading load. U K West cannot host a zone-redundant design, which will matter when the course plans disaster recovery. And both Regions keep the data in the U K. Next, who owns, pays for and governs what the platform puts in those Regions.

Every resource in Azure sits in a hierarchy, and each level of it answers a different question. Read the tree on the left from the top. The tenant is Woodgrove's Microsoft Entra I D, woodgrovebank dot example. It holds every identity: people, groups and applications. Everything below trusts it to say who is asking. Under it is a management group called woodgrove. A management group holds no resources itself; it carries rules and access that flow down to every subscription beneath it, so a policy set here reaches all of them. Woodgrove has two below it. The platform group holds the platform connectivity subscription, where the shared hub network will live. The landing zones group holds the workloads: risk prod and risk dev. A subscription is where money and limits live. It is billed as a unit, it has its own quotas, and it is a hard line for access: someone with rights in risk dev has none in risk prod unless they are granted them. Inside risk prod are resource groups, one for the network, one for the data and one for the applications. A resource group holds resources that are created and deleted together. The table on the right puts that in four lines. The tenant decides who exists. A management group decides rules and access for many subscriptions. A subscription decides who pays, what quotas apply, and draws a hard access line. A resource group decides what lives and dies together. The list beneath names four things a resource group is not. It is not a network boundary: resources in it can still talk to anything the network allows. It is not a billing account: the subscription pays, although costs can be grouped by resource group. It is not a Region: its location only says where its own metadata lives, and its resources can be anywhere. And it is not safe to delete casually, because deleting it deletes everything inside. The last table gives the identifiers this course uses. They are placeholders in the style Microsoft's documentation uses, never real ones. Next, how a request to change any of this reaches Azure.

However you ask Azure to change something, the request arrives at the same place. Along the top of the left side are the clients: the portal in a browser, the Azure C L I, PowerShell, the S D Ks for every language, and Bicep templates. They look different, but each one sends the same kind of H T T P S request, with a token, to one address: management dot azure dot com. That is Azure Resource Manager, often shortened to A R M. Resource Manager runs four checks on every request, the chips in the middle. It validates the Microsoft Entra token, so it knows who is asking. It checks role-based access control, so it knows whether that identity may perform this action on this resource. It applies Azure Policy, so a request that breaks a rule, like creating something outside the U K, is refused. And it honours locks, which can forbid deleting or changing a resource at all. Only then does it pass the request to a resource provider: Microsoft dot Storage for storage accounts, Microsoft dot Network for networks, Microsoft dot DataFactory for pipelines. A provider has to be registered in a subscription before its resources can be created there. All of this is the control plane: creating, configuring and deleting resources. The table on the right sets it beside the data plane, which is using a resource once it exists. Creating the lake account is control plane; reading a file in it is data plane. The control plane is always management dot azure dot com; the data plane is the resource's own address, such as the storage account's blob endpoint. Resource Manager does the checking for the control plane; the service itself checks the data plane. Control-plane permissions are role-based access actions, while data-plane permissions are separate data actions, or a key. And control-plane changes are written to the Activity Log, while data access is logged by each service, if you turn that on. The list underneath draws the consequences. The portal is not special. Anything clicked can be scripted, and anything scripted can be declared in a template. And owning a resource does not mean being able to read its data, which course four shows with a real denial. Next, one request taken apart.

Here is one request taken apart, against the platform's own storage account. The terminal on the right is a real run of the real Azure C L I and the Azure S D K for Python, against the storage emulator, Azurite, so it is labelled emulated. The emulator stands in for the lake account, which is why the lake is lit on the map although the platform builds it in the next course. The first command asks for the hierarchy file in the landing container, the file the bank delivers at six each evening, and prints its size: five hundred and seven bytes. The second runs a short Python script that makes the same read through the S D K and prints the parts of the request as it was sent. It is an H T T P HEAD request, which asks for a file's properties without its contents. The U R L is the storage account's own blob endpoint, followed by the container and the file's name: the data plane. The terminal shows Azure's real address; the replay translates the emulator's local address back into it. The A P I version, sent in a header called x m s version, tells the service which version of its contract the client expects. The date header fixes when the request was made. The scheme is SharedKey, and the account is stwgriskprod: the client signed the request with the account's key, and the signature, a forty four character H M A C, is never printed. The service answered two hundred, O K, and five hundred and seven bytes. The third command asks Resource Manager about the same storage account, the control plane, and it fails before sending anything: please run az login. The control plane does not accept account keys at all; it wants a Microsoft Entra token. The table beneath sets the two side by side. The data plane went to the account's address, named a container and a file, carried a date-based service version, proved itself with an H M A C of the request made with the key. The control plane would go to management dot azure dot com, name the subscription, resource group and account, carry an api version in the query string, and prove itself with a signed Entra token. The list at the bottom draws the lessons. A data-plane call never touches Resource Manager. An account key opens every file in the account, which is why course seven switches keys off. The control plane only takes Entra tokens, and course three signs in to get one. And every request names the version of the contract it expects. Next, how those long names are built.

Every resource in Azure has one full name, its resource I D, and it is the path Resource Manager uses to find it. On the left is the I D of the landing container, split onto one line per part so it can be read; in practice it is one long string. It starts with the subscription, by its identifier. Then the resource group, r g risk prod data. Then the provider, Microsoft dot Storage, and the type and name of the resource: storage accounts, stwgriskprod. That much is the storage account's own I D. A resource can contain child resources, and their I Ds simply continue the path: the account's blob service, called default, and inside it the container named landing. The table beneath reads it from the top. The subscription says who pays and whose quotas apply. The resource group says what lives and dies together. The provider says which service handles it. The type and name are the resource. And the children are resources inside it. On the right are the platform's names, all following one rule: a short type, the letters w g for Woodgrove, the role, and the environment. The resource group is r g risk prod data, the key vault k v w g risk prod, the event hubs namespace e v h w g risk prod, the Databricks workspace d b w w g risk prod, the PostgreSQL server p s q l w g riskmart prod, and the web app app w g exposure prod. The storage account breaks the rule, and the list beneath explains why. A storage account's name becomes part of its address on the internet, so it must be unique across all of Azure, and it may only have three to twenty four lowercase letters and digits: no hyphens. Most names cannot be changed after creation; renaming means creating a new resource and moving to it, which is why the rule is fixed now. And the I D is what everything else points at: scripts, role assignments and policies all name resources by it. Next, what the platform costs while it sits there.

A cloud bill is a sum of meters, and some of them keep running when nothing is happening. On the left is the rate card this course uses. Its numbers are hypothetical, chosen to be easy to follow, and every frame that uses them says so. A virtual machine bills per hour while it is allocated. A managed disk bills per gigabyte per month, whether its machine runs or not. A public I P address bills per hour. An Event Hubs throughput unit bills per hour. Lake storage bills per gigabyte per month, a PostgreSQL server per hour, and log data per gigabyte as it arrives. The list beneath names the traps. A virtual machine shut down from inside its own operating system is still allocated to you, and still billed as if it ran. Disks and static I P addresses bill even when the machine is fully deallocated. Throughput units bill whether or not a single event flows. And a stopped PostgreSQL flexible server starts itself again after seven days, so stopping it is not a way to park it. On the right is one month of the development subscription, risk dev, seven hundred and thirty hours, three ways. Running, the integration machine costs one hundred and forty six dollars, its disk twelve eighty, its public address three sixty five, one throughput unit twenty one ninety and two hundred gigabytes in the lake four dollars: one hundred and eighty eight thirty five in all. Shut down from inside its operating system, the machine is still allocated, so the month is exactly the same. Only when it is deallocated does its line drop to zero, and even then the month is forty two thirty five, because the disk, the address, the throughput unit and the stored data carry on. The habits underneath follow. Deallocate, do not just shut down. Delete what nobody needs, and when everything in a resource group belongs together, delete the group. Tag every resource with an owner and an environment, so every line on a bill has someone to ask. And read the meter before the bill: the next course sets a budget on day one. That completes the picture of how Azure runs; next, the project itself.

From this course on, the platform is a real project, in one folder called risk on azure, and every lesson changes it by one step. Here it is finished, in the frame every lesson after this one uses: the project on the left as an editor shows it, a file in the middle with a terminal underneath, and notes on the right. Today the middle holds a table instead of a file, because this is the tour. Read it from the top. env dot sh and the dot venv folder are where every session starts: the default Region, the default resource group, the storage account, the line that points the tools at an emulator, and the Azure S D Ks for Python. The infra folder holds the Azure C L I scripts that build the platform by hand in courses three to five. The policies folder says who may do what and what may be created at all, from course four on. Templates and pipeline hold the same resources declared in Bicep, and the workflow that deploys them, from course six. Sources holds samples of what the bank delivers: TradeBook rows, the hierarchy file, collateral, limits and price ticks. A D F holds the Data Factory pipelines, stream the producer and consumers for the market feed, and databricks the workspace's Azure side. Serve holds the risk mart's tables and loads; api, functions and filer are what the risk team touches; ops holds queries, alerts, runbooks and drills. Tools holds the calculations: exposure, costs and the models the course uses where an emulator cannot show something. Docs, at the end, holds the decision record. On the right is how to read every lesson. The left panel is the project. New marks a file the lesson adds. The middle is the file, with this lesson's lines highlighted, and below it the terminal exactly as it ran. A pane marked emulated ran against a local emulator, not Azure. And a line that says some number of lines folds what this lesson does not need. Next, the tenant this project will live in, and the accounts that guard it.

Before anything is built, the most powerful accounts in the tenant need putting away. On the left is Woodgrove's tenant and the three kinds of identity in it. At the top are two break-glass accounts. They hold the Global Administrator role, which controls the tenant itself, and they are used only in an emergency, such as everyone else being locked out. Below them are the daily accounts: priya, the data engineer who builds the platform, omar, a risk analyst, and sam, a credit officer. None of them holds an administrator role all the time. At the bottom are workloads: Data Factory, the A P I and the rest will act with identities of their own, not with a person's, and course four creates them. The table on the right says why the top is guarded. A Global Administrator can change any setting in Entra I D and grant any Entra role. A Global Administrator can also elevate themselves to manage access to every subscription in the tenant at once. An Owner of a subscription can do anything inside it, including granting access to others. And priya, on a normal day, can do only what her group is granted. The first list is how to lock the break-glass accounts away, following Microsoft's guidance. Keep two, so one lost credential does not lock the bank out. Make them cloud-only, not federated with the bank's own directory, so they work even when that directory is down. Protect them with phishing-resistant M F A, such as a hardware key, kept apart from the password. Alert on every sign-in and have a person read the alert. And write down, and test, who may open them and when. The last list is why nobody works as one. A daily account will one day be phished, and that must not hand over the tenant. Administrator rights can be granted for an hour when needed instead of held for ever, which course four sets up. Azure requires M F A for portal and C L I sign-ins anyway. And unlike some clouds, Azure has no single root user to fall back on: access is always a role at a scope. Next, priya's first session.

Priya's first job with the Azure C L I is to sign in and make sure her commands will land in the right place. The table in the middle of the right side is what a z login does. It opens a browser, or on a machine without one it prints a short code to type on another device. Priya signs in to Microsoft Entra I D with her M F A. Entra issues tokens the C L I can present to Azure. The C L I lists every subscription she can see in a file called azure profile dot json, in a folder named dot azure in her home directory, and it caches the tokens beside it, refreshing them silently. The terminal above runs the real C L I, but it cannot run that sign-in, because there is no Woodgrove tenant behind this course. Instead the replay places the profile file a z login would write, with no token behind it, and every command in the terminal reads only that file. That is exactly what they do on a real machine too. The first command lists the subscriptions she can see: risk prod, marked default, and risk dev. Every command she runs will land in the default subscription, and production is not where a first experiment belongs, so the second command sets risk dev as the default. The third shows the session: the subscription, the tenant, Woodgrove Bank, and the user, priya at woodgrovebank dot example. The last prints the subscription's identifier, the placeholder from course two. The list at the bottom says what this session is and is not. The default subscription decides where commands land, so set it first, every time. An access token lasts sixty to ninety minutes by default, and the C L I refreshes it while its longer-lived refresh token is valid. a z account show only reads a local file; Azure itself checks the token on every single request, which is why a stale or stolen file is not enough to use. And being signed in grants nothing by itself: what priya may do comes from roles, the subject of the next course. Next, the emulators that stand in for Azure in this course.

This course has no Azure subscription behind it, so every terminal you see runs the real tools against something local, and this lesson shows how. In the editor is env dot sh, which every session sources first. Its first lines set the C L I's defaults: the U K South Region, the development resource group, and the development storage account, s t w g risk dev. The highlighted export below them is the emulator line. It gives the C L I and the S D Ks a connection string that points at Azurite, Microsoft's storage emulator, running on this machine, with Azurite's own account key, which exists nowhere else. Against Azure you would delete that export, sign in, and tell storage commands to use your Entra identity instead of a key. Nothing else in the project changes. The terminal shows the emulator answering like the service. The account starts with no containers. Creating one called scratch returns created true, and deleting it returns deleted true. And asking for a container named Scratch, with a capital S, is refused with the same error Azure gives: invalid characters, because container names must be lowercase. The side table lists the emulators the course uses, all from Microsoft where one exists. Azurite for blobs, queues and tables, from now. The Event Hubs emulator for the market feed and the Service Bus emulator for deal steps, from course nine. The Cosmos D B emulator for the group lookup in course eleven. And real PostgreSQL sixteen for TradeBook and the risk mart, from course eight. The list beneath is what none of them can show: Resource Manager, so no resource group and no role assignment; Entra sign-ins and tokens; packets, private links and failover; quotas and prices. The last list is how the course uses them. The real C L I and S D Ks, with only the endpoint changed. Every pane run against an emulator says emulated. Files that only Azure's control plane could run are checked against Azure's own definitions instead, and say so. And the emulator's key is on screen because it is not a secret; a real key never is. Next, the platform's first real resources.

The platform's first resources are the development lake: a resource group, a storage account, and a container for files as they arrive. They are in the script at the top of the right side, infra slash zero one lake dot sh. It starts by stopping at the first error, and by naming the tags every resource gets: the application, the environment and the owner. The two highlighted Resource Manager commands create the group in U K South, and the storage account inside it. Read the account's settings in the table at the bottom. Hierarchical namespace true makes it a data lake, Azure Data Lake Storage, with real folders, which the lake needs from course seven. Standard L R S keeps three copies in one datacentre, enough for development. Public blob access is off and the minimum T L S version is one point two, safe defaults said out loud rather than assumed. And the tags give every line on a bill an owner. The last highlighted line is different: it creates the landing container through the account's own endpoint, the data plane, signing in with priya's Entra identity rather than a key. Every line of this script has been checked against the Azure C L I's own definition of each command and parameter. In the terminal it runs for real, and stops at the first line, because Resource Manager needs a sign-in this course cannot have. The data-plane step can run, against the emulator, so the next command creates the landing container there: created true. Running the same command again is not an error: created false. That matters, because a script that is safe to run twice can be run again after a failure without making a mess, which is a habit every script in this course keeps. The last command lists the account's containers: landing, created at the frozen time this replay runs at. On the map, the lake now has its colour. Next, what this costs, how to see it coming, and how to remove it.

Cost is introduced with the first resource, not after the first bill. In the editor is tools slash cost ledger dot py, a short Python program that prices the development environment's month on the course's hypothetical rate card. Its table lists five lines: the integration machine, its disk, its public address, the Event Hubs namespace and the lake. Each has a quantity, a meter, and the value of its owner tag. One line, the Event Hubs namespace, has no owner: it was made by hand, without tags. The terminal is the program's real run. The five lines come to one hundred and eighty eight thirty five a month while everything runs, forty two thirty five with the machine deallocated, as in course two. Grouped by owner tag, priya's lines are one hundred and sixty six forty five, and twenty one ninety belongs to nobody. Then the budget. The table at the top right is budgets slash risk dev monthly dot json, the project's budget definition: one hundred and fifty dollars a month, filtered to resources tagged environment dev, emailing priya when actual cost passes eighty percent and when the forecast passes one hundred. The ledger's forecast is one hundred and twenty six percent of it, so the budget would send an alert. It would not stop anything. The list beneath says so plainly: a budget is an alarm, not a cap. Deleting the resource group deletes everything inside it, but the last list names what it leaves behind: role assignments and policies granted above the group; logs sent to a workspace in another group; a key vault's name, which Azure holds for ninety days after deletion by default; and budgets, which belong to the subscription. That completes the start of the project; next, locking it down.

Locking the platform down starts with the people who will touch it, and the identity service that says who they are: Microsoft Entra I D, now lit on the map. At the top right is infra slash zero four groups dot sh. It creates four groups in Entra I D, one for each kind of person who touches risk data, and adds priya to hers. Every permission in this course will be granted to a group, never to a person, so that when someone joins or leaves, only their membership changes. The script's lines have been checked against the Azure C L I's own definitions; like every Entra and Resource Manager command in this course, they cannot run without a real tenant. The table beneath names the groups. Risk Data Engineers, with priya, build the platform. Risk Analysts, with omar, read exposure and trends. Credit Officers, with sam, receive breach alerts and own the limits. And Risk Auditors read reports and logs, and change nothing. The daily accounts in these groups are not created by hand: they are synchronised from the bank's own directory, so a leaver disabled there is disabled here. The break-glass accounts from course three are the exception, cloud-only on purpose. The second table is Conditional Access, Entra's set of rules applied at sign-in, which needs an Entra I D P one licence. Anyone holding an administrator role must use phishing-resistant M F A. Analysts and credit officers reach risk data only from a compliant bank device. Old sign-in protocols that cannot do M F A are blocked for everyone. And the two break-glass accounts are excluded from any rule that blocks sign-in, so a broken policy cannot lock the bank out. The list at the bottom separates two questions this course keeps apart. Authentication asks who you are, and Entra I D answers it, with passwords, M F A and these rules. Authorisation asks what you may do, here, and roles answer it, which is most of this course. Next, how an application, rather than a person, gets an identity and a token.

People sign in; applications are registered. The project gains infra slash zero four app dot sh, summarised in the first table on the right. It registers the exposure A P I, which creates two things. The application object is the definition: its name, and the identifier tokens will carry, a p i colon slash slash exposure a p i. The service principal is that application's identity inside Woodgrove's tenant, the thing that can be granted access. In the editor is tools slash token claims dot py, which shows what a token is. When omar opens the risk dashboard and it calls the exposure A P I for him, Entra I D issues an access token: a signed J S O N document. The program builds one with the same claims Entra uses, but signs it with a key made on this machine, because there is no tenant behind this course; the list at the bottom of the right side says so. The audience claim, a u d, says who the token is for: the exposure A P I. The issuer and tenant claims say Woodgrove's tenant issued it. o i d identifies omar. s c p holds the delegated permission he consented to, Exposure dot Read. And a z p names the dashboard application that asked for it. The terminal is a real run of the real library. The token is eight hundred and twenty one characters in three parts: a header, the claims, and a signature. Decoding it with the issuer's public key verifies the signature and prints the claims. It lasts sixty five minutes, inside the sixty to ninety minutes Entra gives by default. Then the program changes one claim, Read to Admin, and verification fails: anyone can read a token's claims, but nobody can change them without the issuer's private key. The middle table is what the exposure A P I must check on every call: the signature against Entra's published key, that the audience is itself, that the issuer is Woodgrove's tenant, that it has not expired, and that the scope or role allows the operation. Next, identities for workloads that never sign in at all.

Data Factory, the exposure A P I and the rest of the platform need identities too, and giving each one a password to store would create the very secrets the bank most wants to avoid. Managed identities solve that, and they are now lit on the map. A managed identity is a service principal that Azure creates and whose credentials Azure rotates. Code running on the resource asks a local endpoint for a token and never sees a secret at all. The script at the top, infra slash zero four identities dot sh, creates one user-assigned identity, i d w g exposure prod, and assigns it to the exposure A P I's web app; course twelve also gives it to the breach alert function, so both share one identity. The comments note that Data Factory and the Databricks access connector get system-assigned ones, made with them in courses eight and ten. The first table lists the platform's workload identities and how each one ends. The user-assigned identity lives until someone deletes it on purpose. The factory's, the connector's and the integration machine's are system-assigned, so each disappears with its resource. The second table compares the two kinds. A system-assigned identity belongs to one resource, cannot be shared, and is deleted with it. A user-assigned identity belongs to itself, can be shared by many resources, and is deleted only on purpose, which makes it simpler to grant access before the resource exists, and to keep the same access when a resource is rebuilt. Microsoft now recommends user-assigned identities for its own services for those reasons. The list at the bottom sets the limits. There is no secret to store, leak or rotate, because Azure handles the credential. But an identity grants nothing by itself: until it is given a role, it can read nothing, which the next lesson does. And only Azure resources can use a managed identity, so TradeBook, in the bank's data centre, will need a different arrangement in course eight. Next, the roles that give these identities, and the bank's groups, their access.

Azure decides what an identity may do with role-based access control. The first table on the right shows that a role assignment has three parts: who, which role, and where, its scope. In the editor is policies slash assignments dot py, the platform's assignments written down. The scopes at the top are real resource I Ds: the landing zones management group, the two subscriptions, the prod data resource group, the lake, and its containers. Below them are the assignments. Risk Data Engineers are Contributors on the whole development subscription and Readers on production. Risk Analysts hold Storage Blob Data Reader on the gold container only. Risk Auditors are Readers across the landing zones management group, and Blob Data Readers on the reports container. Data Factory's identity may write to the landing container. The roles themselves are Azure's built-in definitions, copied word for word from Microsoft's documentation into policies slash roles. The terminal runs tools slash access table dot py, which asks a small model of Azure's rules who may do what. It is a model, not Azure, and the next lesson shows its rules. priya may create a virtual machine in risk dev, because Contributor on the subscription reaches every resource group inside it. She may not grant a role there: Contributor excludes writing role assignments, so the answer names the exclusion. She may read the production lake's settings, as a Reader, and may not change them. omar may read a file in gold, and not one in landing. The auditor reads the production lake's settings through Reader held at the management group, two levels above it. And Data Factory may write to landing and not to gold. The second table is the rule that produced those answers: a role held at a scope reaches everything beneath it, from management group to subscription to resource group to resource and its children. The habits at the bottom follow from it. Assign roles to groups, not people. Use the smallest scope that works. And prefer built-in roles to custom ones, because Microsoft maintains them as services change. Next, the line between managing a resource and reading its data.

Here is the rule from course two, enforced. In the editor is the heart of tools slash access check dot py, the model the last lesson used. Every role definition has two lists of permissions: actions, for managing a resource, and data actions, for reading and writing what is inside it. The check picks the right list for the request, finds an assignment whose scope covers the target, and allows the request only if the role grants it and does not exclude it. The first table on the right sets the two lists side by side. Contributor has every action, and no data actions at all. Storage Blob Data Reader has one data action: reading blobs. The terminal runs tools slash planes dot py. In it, an incident fix has given priya Contributor on the production data resource group. She may now change the lake's settings. But when she tries to read a file in gold with her Entra identity, she is denied: Contributor manages the account and cannot read a byte of it. omar, with Storage Blob Data Reader, may read the same file, and may not change a single setting. So far that is the separation working. The third line is the catch, and the reason the first list on the right exists. Contributor may list the storage account's keys, because listing keys is a management action. And an account key authorises every data operation in the account, whoever holds it, with no role and no Entra sign-in involved. A Contributor who wants to read the data can, through the back door. The fix is not a role: it is a setting on the account, allow shared key access false, which makes Azure Storage refuse every request signed with a key. The lake gets it in course seven, and from then on, Entra identities and data roles are the only way in. The last list repeats that this is a model: the role definitions are real, word for word, and so are the scope rules, but it leaves out deny assignments and role conditions, which Azure also evaluates. Next, rules about what may be created at all.

Roles decide who may make a change. Azure Policy decides whether a change may be made at all, by anyone, and it is now lit on the map. The platform gets two rules, both assigned to the landing zones management group so they reach both subscriptions. The first is a built-in definition called Allowed locations, kept word for word in policies slash builtin, with an assignment that lists two Regions: U K South and U K West. The second is custom, and it is in the editor: policies slash storage private dot json. Its rule has an if and a then. If the resource's type is a storage account, and its public network access property is anything other than Disabled, then the effect is deny, and Resource Manager refuses the request. The property is named through an alias, the path Azure Policy uses to read a setting from any request. The terminal runs tools slash policy check dot py, a model of the conditions these two rules use, against five proposed resources. The production lake in U K South with public access disabled is allowed. A copy of it in West Europe is denied by Allowed locations. A scratch account in U K South with public access enabled is denied by the storage rule. A temporary account in U K West that does not mention public access at all is also denied, because a missing property is not equal to Disabled, which is why every template in this course states that setting. And a resource group in West Europe is allowed. That last line is not a mistake in the model: Allowed locations runs in Indexed mode, which evaluates resources and not resource groups, and Microsoft provides a separate built-in for groups. The tables on the right separate Policy from role-based access: role-based access asks whether this person may do it, Policy asks whether anyone may make this. And the list at the bottom says what compliance does not prove. A policy checks only what its rules name. It knows nothing about code, data or people. And a gap, like the resource group, passes quietly. Next, how management groups and subscriptions separate production from everything else.

The policies and roles of the last three lessons were assigned at management groups, and this lesson builds the groups they hang on. The script at the top right, infra slash zero four management groups dot sh, creates woodgrove, and two groups under it: platform and landing zones. It places the platform connectivity subscription, home of the shared hub network, under platform, and both risk subscriptions, prod and dev, under landing zones. This is the shape Microsoft's landing-zone guidance recommends: the platform that many workloads share, kept apart from the workloads that use it. The first table shows what each level adds as rules flow down. Assigned at woodgrove, the U K-only and no-public-storage policies reach every subscription the bank will ever create. The platform group adds ownership by the platform team. The landing zones group adds the auditors' read access, which is why the auditor in the last lesson could read the production lake. The second table answers what a subscription actually isolates. Its bill and budget, yes. Its quotas, yes. Its role assignments, yes, apart from those inherited from a management group above. Its network, no: a virtual network in one subscription can be peered with a virtual network in another, so a subscription is not a network boundary, any more than a resource group is. Course five draws the network boundaries properly. The list at the bottom says why production and development are two subscriptions rather than two resource groups. A mistake in development, a deleted group or a runaway script, cannot touch production's resources, because nobody working in dev holds a role in prod beyond reading it. Production can be held to stricter rules, with fewer people and more policies, without slowing development down. And each has its own bill, quotas and limits, so a test that exhausts a quota in dev does not stop the overnight run in prod. Next, the most powerful access of all, and who keeps the record of it.

Sooner or later someone needs real power over production: priya, during an incident, needs Owner on risk prod for an hour. The left side is how that happens without anyone holding Owner permanently. With Privileged Identity Management, P I M, the role is assigned to priya as eligible: hers to switch on, but switched off. When she needs it, she asks to activate it, with M F A, a justification and the incident's ticket number. Another person, the platform lead, approves; priya cannot approve herself. The role is then active for one hour, and switches itself off. Every step is logged, in Entra's audit log and in Azure's Activity Log. The table at the top of the middle is the other half of keeping access small: access reviews. Every quarter, each group's owner is asked to confirm, person by person, who still needs to be in it. Risk Data Engineers are reviewed by the platform lead, Risk Analysts by the head of risk, Risk Auditors by internal audit, and every eligible Owner by the security team. Anyone not confirmed is removed. On the far right is the result for Owner on risk prod: nobody holds it all the time; three platform engineers are eligible for an hour at a time, with approval; and the two break-glass accounts can reach it through Global Administrator. The middle table beneath the reviews is the landing-zone boundary from the last lesson, as ownership. The platform team owns the management groups and Policy, the hub network and D N S, and the central logs and audit trail. The risk team owns its two subscriptions, its spoke network and subnets, and its own diagnostics. The list at the bottom is about the audit trail. The Activity Log keeps control-plane events for ninety days and then deletes them, so they must be exported to keep them longer. They go to a workspace the risk team cannot delete, because the people being audited must not own the record of what they did. And both P I M and access reviews need Entra I D P two or I D Governance licences, which a bank of this size would hold, and a smaller organisation should check. That completes locking the platform down; next, giving it a private network.

Before the platform gets a network, it needs an address plan, and the plan has to fit around the bank's own network, which already exists. In the editor is tools slash c i d r plan dot py. A range is written in C I D R form: an address, a slash, and a prefix length that says how many leading bits name the network. The table at the top right reads four of them. Slash twenty is four thousand and ninety six addresses: the production spoke. Slash twenty four is two hundred and fifty six: the subnet for private endpoints. Slash twenty six is sixty four: one ordinary subnet. And slash twenty eight, sixteen, is the smallest Azure allows. The plan in the editor lists the bank's on-premises network, ten fifty slash sixteen; the hub network the platform team runs, ten one hundred slash twenty two, with subnets for the ExpressRoute gateway, the firewall and an inbound D N S resolver; the production spoke, ten one ten slash twenty, with subnets for Databricks, private endpoints, the app and the integration runtime; and the development spoke beside it. The terminal is its real run. Every subnet is checked to sit inside its network, and its usable addresses are counted, which is always five fewer than its size, because Azure reserves the first four addresses and the last one in every subnet. A slash twenty six has fifty nine usable, a slash twenty seven twenty seven. The last line is the check that matters most: no range overlaps another. These networks will all be joined, the spokes to the hub and the hub to the bank, and two overlapping ranges cannot be routed between: one of them would have to be renumbered, which is painful once anything runs in it. The second table lists the ports the platform uses: four four three for H T T P S, to storage and A P Is; five four three two for PostgreSQL; nine zero nine three for the Kafka endpoint of Event Hubs; and twenty two for S S H, closed to everyone. The rules at the bottom follow: no overlap with anything the network will ever join, room to grow, and one range per environment. Next, the spoke itself.

With the plan agreed, infra slash zero five network dot sh builds the production spoke, and the virtual network is now lit on the map. A virtual network lives in one Region and holds subnets; every machine, endpoint or service that joins it gets an address in one of them. The script creates v net risk prod u k s with the slash twenty range, then five subnets through a small helper. Every subnet is created with default outbound access off. That is now Azure's own default for new networks, since the A P I versions released after the end of March twenty twenty six: a private subnet has no automatic way to the internet, so anything that needs to go out must take a route the bank chose, which is the next lesson. Two subnets are delegated to Azure Databricks, which needs a pair, one for each side of a cluster node, each at least a slash twenty six. One is delegated to App Service, for the exposure A P I's outbound calls into the network. The private-endpoint subnet and the integration-runtime subnet are not delegated. The table at the bottom says what lives where. Like every network command in this course, the script has been checked against the Azure C L I's own definitions, and cannot run without a subscription. The terminal runs a sizing model instead, tools slash subnet fit dot py, because subnets are hard to change: a delegated subnet in use cannot be resized. Each Databricks subnet needs one address per cluster node, so the overnight run's sixteen workers and a driver need seventeen of fifty nine. The private-endpoint subnet needs one per endpoint, nine of two hundred and fifty one. The app subnet is the tightest: App Service briefly doubles the addresses a plan uses while it scales, so ten instances can need twenty of fifty nine. The integration runtime needs two of twenty seven. Every subnet has room to roughly treble, which is the headroom this plan was sized for. Next, where traffic from these subnets goes.

Every subnet has an effective route table, and Azure chooses a route for each packet by a simple rule: the longest matching prefix wins, and between routes with the same prefix, a route you define beats one learned by B G P, which beats a system route. The terminal runs tools slash route pick dot py, a model of that rule, for a packet leaving the A P I's subnet to three places. Without a route table of its own, a packet for the lake's private endpoint, ten one ten one four, matches the spoke's own range and stays local. A packet for TradeBook, ten fifty twelve seven, matches the bank's range, which the ExpressRoute gateway learned by B G P, so it goes to the gateway. A packet for a public package site matches only the default route, nought nought nought nought slash nought, and in a private subnet that leads nowhere: there is no default outbound access. The script at the top, infra slash zero five routes dot sh, adds the bank's choice: a route table with one user-defined route, nought nought nought nought slash nought, to a virtual appliance, the hub firewall at ten one hundred nought sixty eight, associated with the app, integration runtime and endpoint subnets. Run the model again, and the first two answers do not change, because their prefixes are longer than slash nought. Only the internet-bound packet changes: it now goes to the firewall, as a user-defined route, where the platform team inspects it and lets through only what is approved. The table at the bottom lists the ways out of a private subnet. A route to a firewall, which production uses, because the bank inspects all egress. A NAT gateway, which gives many machines one stable outbound address, cheaper and simpler, which development uses. A public I P on a machine, which is rarely right, because it is also a way in. Or nothing at all, the safest choice if nothing needs to go out. Next, the filters that decide which of these packets are allowed in.

Routes decide where a packet goes; a network security group decides whether it may arrive. The script at the top, infra slash zero five n s g dot sh, protects the private-endpoint subnet, where the lake, the vault, Event Hubs and the risk mart will have their addresses. A small helper creates inbound rules from a name, a priority, a source, a port and an allow or deny. The A P I's subnet may reach port five four three two, the risk mart. Databricks' two subnets, written as one slash twenty five, may reach four four three, the lake. The integration runtime may reach four four three too. And at priority four thousand and ninety six, everything else from the virtual network is denied. The terminal runs tools slash n s g check dot py, a model of how Azure evaluates those rules, against six flows. Rules are read from the lowest priority number up, and the first one that matches decides. The A P I reaching the mart matches rule one hundred: allowed. A Databricks node reaching the lake matches one ten. The integration machine reaching the lake matches one twenty. The same machine reaching the mart matches nothing until four thousand and ninety six: denied, because it has no reason to. TradeBook, on the bank's network, is denied in the same way. And a request from the internet falls all the way to the default rule at sixty five thousand five hundred, deny all inbound. The rule at four thousand and ninety six is the one people forget, and the list at the bottom says why. Azure adds default rules beneath yours, and one of them, allow V Net inbound, lets in the whole virtual network service tag: this network, every peered network and the bank's own ranges. Without an explicit deny above it, every machine on the bank's network could reach the endpoints. The rules are also stateful: a reply to an allowed request goes back out without a rule of its own. And on Databricks' delegated subnets, Databricks adds the rules its clusters need, which are left alone. Next, how a name like the lake's turns into one of these private addresses.

Code never connects to ten one ten one four; it connects to s t w g risk prod dot blob dot core dot windows dot net, and D N S decides which address that name means. The trick that makes private endpoints work without changing any code is in the terminal, which runs tools slash resolve dot py, a model of the same name resolved from three places. For a laptop on the internet, the name is a C N A M E, an alias, to s t w g risk prod dot privatelink dot blob dot core dot windows dot net, and public D N S resolves that to a public address. For the A P I, inside the spoke, the first step is the same alias. But the spoke is linked to a private D N S zone with exactly that privatelink name, and the zone answers with the private endpoint's address, ten one ten one four. The same name, two answers, depending on where you ask. TradeBook, on the bank's network, gets the private answer too, by a longer path: the bank's own D N S servers forward anything under core dot windows dot net to an inbound endpoint of a D N S private resolver in the hub, and the hub is linked to the zone. The script at the top, infra slash zero five d n s dot sh, creates the five private zones the platform needs, for blobs, the data lake endpoint, Key Vault, Service Bus and Event Hubs, and PostgreSQL, and links each one to the spoke and to the hub. Auto-registration is off, because these zones only ever hold private endpoints' records. The table at the bottom names the three pieces: public D N S, which answers the internet with a public address; the private zone, which answers linked networks with the private one; and the hub's resolver, which lets the bank's D N S ask Azure. Most private-endpoint problems turn out to be D N S problems: a network not linked, or a forwarder missing, quietly sends traffic to the public address, which the next lessons switch off. Next, encryption along the path.

A private network keeps traffic away from the internet. It does not make it unreadable, and this lesson separates the two. T L S encrypts one hop, between the two ends that run it; every later hop needs its own. The first table on the right walks the platform's paths hop by hop. An analyst's browser reaches Front Door over T L S with the bank's certificate, and Front Door ends that session. Front Door opens a new T L S session to the exposure A P I, which App Service ends. The A P I reaches the risk mart over T L S, which PostgreSQL flexible server requires by default. Databricks reaches the lake over H T T P S, with T L S one point two as the minimum. Then the row that matters: TradeBook's data travels from the bank to the integration machine over ExpressRoute, and ExpressRoute traffic is not encrypted by default. It is private, carried by a provider and never on the internet, but it is not secret. Microsoft offers MACsec only on ExpressRoute Direct, where the bank owns the ports, and IPsec can be run over a circuit. The last hop, from the integration machine to the lake, is H T T P S again. The second table lists the certificates involved. The dashboard's name, risk dot woodgrovebank dot example, has a certificate from a public certificate authority, kept in Key Vault from course six. App Service's default domain has Microsoft's. And the PostgreSQL server presents one chained to Microsoft's root, which clients should verify. The list at the bottom draws the lesson. A private endpoint keeps traffic off the internet, not unreadable. ExpressRoute carries plain text unless MACsec or IPsec is added. So TradeBook's copy in course eight is wrapped in T L S from end to end by the database connection itself. And the minimum T L S version is set on every service, never assumed. Next, the private endpoints themselves.

Private endpoints, now lit on the map, give each service an address inside the spoke, and then the public one can be switched off. The script at the top, infra slash zero five private endpoints dot sh, looks up the lake's resource I D, then creates two private endpoints in the endpoint subnet: one for blobs and one for the data lake's own endpoint, called d f s, because each sub-resource of a service gets its own. Each endpoint gets a D N S zone group, which writes its record into the matching private zone from two lessons ago, so the names resolve with no further work. The last command is the point of all of it: public network access on the lake is disabled. From then on, the storage account refuses every request that does not arrive through a private endpoint. The terminal runs tools slash reach dot py, a model of who can still reach the lake. A laptop on the internet resolves the public address and is refused: public network access is disabled. The A P I in the spoke resolves the private address, has a route to it, and reaches the lake, and then a role decides the rest, as course four showed. TradeBook, over ExpressRoute with the bank's D N S forwarding, reaches it too. And a machine in the development network, which is not peered with production, resolves the public address and is refused, which is the separation course four wanted. The table at the bottom compares the older alternative, the service endpoint. A service endpoint keeps the service's public address, and lets the service's firewall recognise traffic from chosen subnets. It cannot be reached from on-premises, it cannot coexist with public access switched fully off, and it costs nothing extra. A private endpoint gives a private address, works from on-premises over ExpressRoute, allows public access to be switched off, and is charged per hour and per gigabyte. For a bank's data, the private endpoint is the choice, and every data service in this course gets one. Next, what stands in front of the exposure dashboard.

Something has to stand in front of the exposure dashboard, and Azure offers four kinds of thing, each in a column at the top. Azure Load Balancer works at layer four: it spreads T C P and U D P connections by port, within one Region, inside a network or in public, and knows nothing about U R Ls, certificates or attacks. Application Gateway works at layer seven, for H T T P: within one Region, it routes by host name and path, ends T L S, and can carry a web application firewall; its front end can be private, inside the network, or public. Front Door is also layer seven, but global: requests arrive at Microsoft's nearest edge location, where Front Door can cache, filter with a firewall and end T L S, then travel Microsoft's network to the origin. Its front end is always public, but the origin behind it can be private, reached over Private Link. Traffic Manager is different again: it only answers D N S, sending each lookup to a Region by a rule or a health probe, and carries no traffic at all. The first table below matches them to what the dashboard needs. It is H T T P, chosen by U R L, which rules out Load Balancer. It needs T L S and a firewall in front, which rules out Traffic Manager. It has readers in London and, soon, Singapore. And the A P I behind it is private, which every remaining choice can reach. The second table is the answer, in two steps. Now, while the dashboard serves London only, and only bank staff on the bank's network, a private Application Gateway in the spoke is the front: regional, layer seven, with a firewall, and no public address at all. In course fourteen, when the Singapore office joins, Front Door takes over, so readers on the far side of the world meet an edge near them, with the private A P I still reached over Private Link. The choice follows the readers, not the other way round. Next, the link that carries the bank's data into all of this.

The last piece of the network joins it to the bank, and ExpressRoute is now lit on the map. The platform uses a hub and spoke: a hub network, owned by the platform team, holds what many workloads share, the ExpressRoute gateway, the firewall and the D N S resolver, and each workload's spoke is peered to it. The script at the top, infra slash zero five peering dot sh, creates that peering in both directions. The spoke's side allows forwarded traffic, so packets the firewall passes on are accepted, and uses the hub's remote gateways, so the spoke reaches the bank through the hub's ExpressRoute gateway without one of its own. The hub's side, in the platform connectivity subscription, allows gateway transit. The table beneath lists the ways to join networks. Virtual network peering joins two networks over Microsoft's backbone, in the same Region or across Regions. ExpressRoute joins the bank to Azure through a connectivity provider, privately, without crossing the public internet. A site-to-site V P N joins them over the internet, inside I P sec. And hub and spoke is a pattern built from peerings and gateway transit, not a separate product. The list at the bottom is what the platform uses and why. An ExpressRoute circuit in London carries TradeBook's nightly copy, with predictable bandwidth and latency. A V P N is configured as its backup through the same hub, so a failed circuit slows the copy instead of stopping it. Peering is not transitive: the development spoke is peered with the hub but not with production, and a packet cannot hop from one spoke to another through the hub unless the hub's firewall routes it, which it is told not to do. And ownership follows the landing-zone boundary from course four: the platform team owns the hub, the risk team owns its spoke. That completes the network; next, making all of this repeatable.

Course five built the spoke with a script, infra slash zero five network dot sh, shown at the top: a virtual network, then five subnets, one command each. A month later, someone needs the app subnet twice as big, and someone else wants the integration runtime subnet gone, so they edit the script and run it again. The terminal runs a model of what happens, tools slash script rerun dot py, because there is no Resource Manager emulator to run the real thing against. Resource Manager creates or updates on every request, so the three subnets that did not change come back unchanged: running a create command twice duplicates nothing. The app subnet is refused, because App Service is joined to it, and a subnet's range cannot change while something uses it. The integration runtime subnet, deleted from the script, is left alone: a script says what to do, never what should exist, so removing a line removes nothing. And a subnet called snet test, which someone added by hand in the portal, is left alone too, because the script never looks at what is there. The table at the bottom names what a script cannot say. You want snet shir gone, and deleting the line does nothing. You want snet test noticed, and the script never looks. You want dev to match prod, and you get a second copy of the script, edited by hand, that slowly drifts. And you want to see a change before it happens, and the only way a script can show you is to run. All four have the same cause: a script describes steps, and the platform needs a description of the end state. Next, Bicep, which is exactly that.

The editor holds templates slash modules slash network dot bicep: the same spoke, written as what should exist instead of the steps to make it. A resource line names a type, Microsoft dot Network slash virtual Networks, and an A P I version, twenty twenty five, zero seven, zero one. The version is a contract: it fixes which properties exist and what they mean, so this file means the same thing in five years. The subnets are declared as child resources, with parent colon v net, in a loop over the subnets parameter, and at batch size one, so they are made one after another, because parallel changes to one network's subnets collide. Bicep is a language for people; Resource Manager reads A R M templates, which are J S O N. The terminal compiles the file with bicep build, and tools slash arm summary dot py lists what the J S O N declares: a deployment template with four parameters, the virtual network at its A P I version, and the subnets, after the virtual network. Bicep worked out that order from the parent reference; nobody wrote it. The first table on the right maps one to the other. The at sign version is the A P I version and its properties. Parent colon v net becomes a child, deployed after its parent. The for loop becomes a copy loop, one per subnet. Batch size one makes the loop go one at a time. And an output, the network's I D, is a value the next module can use. The list underneath is what a deployment does in incremental mode, the default. It creates what is declared and missing, updates what is declared and different, leaves alone anything it does not declare, and is recorded, with a name, its template and its result, so every change to the platform has a history. Next, modules, which put the spoke, the lake and the vault together.

One file per environment would drift as fast as the scripts did, so the platform is one main file built from modules. The editor shows templates slash main dot bicep. Its first line that matters is target Scope equals subscription: this file is deployed to a whole subscription, because it creates the resource groups that everything else lives in. Below that, three modules: the network, the lake and the vault, each its own Bicep file, each given a scope, the net or the data resource group, which this same file creates. A module never says which subscription or group it is in; whoever uses it decides. The terminal compiles main and lists what it declares: two resource groups, then three nested deployments, one per module, each holding its own resources. The network's deployment comes after net, and the lake's and the vault's after data, because each module refers to its group. No depends on was written; a reference is a dependency. The table on the right lists the four scopes a deployment can land in. The tenant, for management groups. A management group, for policies and roles that reach many subscriptions, which is where Course four's guardrails belong. A subscription, for resource groups. And a resource group, for nearly everything else. The list underneath says what a module is: a Bicep file used by another one, which becomes a nested deployment, lands in the scope it is given, waits for whatever it refers to, and is used by dev and prod alike, so the two environments are built by the same code. Next, the values that make one environment different from the other, including a password that must never be written down.

Main dot bicep now has a fourth module, the two integration runtime machines that Course eight will use, and they need an administrator password. The editor shows templates slash prod dot bicep param, the parameter file for production. Its first line, using main dot bicep, ties it to the template. Then the values: env is prod, the address space is ten one ten nought nought slash twenty, then the five subnets. A second file, dev dot bicep param, has the same names with dev's values. The last parameter is the password, and its value is not a password. It is a call to get Secret, naming the production subscription, the data resource group, the vault k v w g risk prod, and a secret called runtime admin password. The terminal compiles the parameter file and shows what Resource Manager receives: not a value, but a reference, a Key Vault I D and a secret name. Resource Manager reads the secret itself, during the deployment, into a parameter marked secure, which is never kept in the deployment's history. Two settings make that work: the vault allows template deployment, which the vault module now sets, and whoever deploys needs permission to use the vault for a deployment, which Contributor includes. The table on the right compares the two parameter files: env, the address space, ten one ten against ten one twenty, the subscription, and which vault the password comes from. The list underneath follows the password. It is in Key Vault, put there once by a person. It is not in the repository, where only its name appears. It is read by Resource Manager while deploying, it is not kept in the history, and the vault allows template deployment. Outputs go the other way: the network module's I D is passed into the runtime module, so the machines land in snet shir without anyone copying an I D. Next, how to see what a deployment will change before it changes it.

Before a deployment changes anything, Resource Manager can say what it would change. The command is a z deployment what if, in infra slash zero six deploy dot sh, and it compares the template with what exists, resource by resource, and changes nothing. Without a subscription, the editor shows a model of that comparison, tools slash what if dot py. Its template holds four of the data group's resources: the lake, the vault and the two runtime machines. What is live differs in two ways. Someone lowered the lake's minimum T L S version to one point nought by hand, and someone made a storage account called s t w g scratch in the portal. The terminal prints the answer in what if's own symbols. The vault, an equals sign: no change. The lake, a tilde: modify, T L S one point nought back to one point two. The two machines, a plus: create. And the scratch account, a star: ignore, because incremental mode leaves alone what the template does not mention. In complete mode, the second block, the same account gets a minus: delete. Complete mode makes the group match the template exactly, which is why it is used rarely and deliberately. The first table on the right is drift, a change made outside the template, and what the next deployment does about it: T L S lowered by hand is put back, the scratch account is ignored or deleted, and a group's tag removed is put back. The second table lists changes that are really a new resource. Any change of name declares a second resource, and the old one stays. A machine's zone is set when it is created, so changing it means rebuilding. A deleted vault's name stays held for ninety days by soft delete. And a subnet in use cannot be resized, as the script found. Next, running all of this from a pipeline, with no password anywhere.

Deployments should come from one place, a pipeline, not from whoever's laptop is open. The editor shows dot github slash workflows slash release dot y m l, the GitHub Actions workflow that releases one environment. A pipeline needs to sign in to Azure, and the old way was a client secret stored in GitHub: a password that works from anywhere, until someone rotates it. This one stores nothing.
