Permissions, i d token write, lets the job ask GitHub for a short lived token that says which repository and environment it is running for. The job names its environment, dev or prod, and prod's environment requires a reviewer to approve before the job starts. The azure slash login step hands GitHub's token to Entra I D, with three identifiers that are not secrets: a client I D, the tenant and the subscription, set separately for each environment. Entra I D trusts that token through a federated credential, which infra slash zero six federation dot sh created: one deployment identity per environment, each trusting one subject, and each a Contributor on its own subscription only. The terminal runs tools slash o i d c subject dot py, a model of the match. The release job for dev gets the subject that ends environment colon dev, and signs in as risk deploy dev. The prod job signs in as risk deploy prod. A pull request gets a subject ending pull request, which no credential names, so it is refused, and so is a fork, whose repository name differs. The match is exact, every part. The table on the right compares the two ways in: a client secret is stored in GitHub, expires when someone sets it, works anywhere if it leaks, and serves whoever holds it. Federation stores nothing, each token lasts minutes, a leak is one job's token, and only one repository's environment can use it. Next, the data code that the same pipeline must release, and the order it lands in.

The platform's infrastructure is not all it releases. Course eight adds Data Factory pipelines, and Course ten adds Databricks jobs, and both are code that must reach production the same way. The card on the right is the release workflow as it will look once they exist, so it is checked against GitHub Actions' rules rather than replayed. It signs in once, the same way, and the Databricks command line uses that same Entra I D sign in. Then three steps, in an order that matters. First, infra slash zero six deploy dot sh: the infrastructure everything runs on. Second, databricks bundle deploy: a Databricks asset bundle declares jobs and the targets they go to, dev or prod, and this deploys the jobs for this environment. Third, Data Factory's release: stop its triggers, deploy, and start them again. The table underneath says why that order. Infrastructure needs nothing, because everything lives in it. The Databricks jobs need the workspace and the lake. And Data Factory needs the jobs its pipelines start: deploy it first, and a pipeline could call a job that is not there yet. The list at the bottom is how Data Factory itself is released. Only the development factory is connected to git, where engineers build pipelines in the browser and save to a branch. A build turns the main branch into an A R M template, with Microsoft's own tool. Test and production factories are deployed from that template and never edited by hand. And triggers stop for the deployment and start again after it, so no run starts halfway through a change. Next, making sure that what reaches production is exactly what dev tested.

If each environment compiles the templates for itself, dev and prod can get different results from the same commit, from a newer tool or a changed module. So the workflow at the top, dot github slash workflows slash deploy dot y m l, now builds once. A build job checks out the commit, runs infra slash zero six build dot sh, and uploads the out folder as an artifact called release. The dev job needs the build, and prod needs dev: prod is promoted, it never builds. Each release job downloads that same artifact rather than rebuilding it. The terminal runs the build script: bicep compiles main to J S O N and each parameter file to its own, and a checksum file records all three. The release script checks those checksums before it deploys, and names the deployment after the commit, so the deployment history in each subscription says which commit made it. That is provenance: from a running resource, back to a deployment, to a commit, to a review. The table at the bottom places Terraform, which many banks use alongside or instead of Bicep. Bicep is Azure only; Terraform describes many clouds in one language. Bicep keeps no state, because Azure itself is the state; Terraform keeps a state file, which must be stored, locked and protected, since it can hold secrets. New Azure A P I versions work in Bicep on the day they are released; in Terraform, the Az A P I provider has them at once and the Azure R M provider later. And both preview a change: Bicep with what if, Terraform with plan. Either is a fair choice; mixing them for the same resources is not. That completes the platform's automation. Next, Course seven lands the daily files in the lake.

Before the platform lands its first file, it helps to know the three ways Azure stores one. The first column is object storage, Blob Storage: a name and its bytes, read and written whole, over H T T P S, in any size and any number. The lake is object storage, with Data Lake Storage's folders on top. The second is file storage, Azure Files: a shared drive with folders, where people open a file and edit it in place, mapped on their desktop as a drive letter. The collateral team will work from one. The third is block storage, managed disks: the blocks under a machine's file system, attached to one virtual machine at a time, small and fast. The integration runtime's machines run on them. The table at the bottom left is what survives what, because each kind fails differently. A machine that restarts loses nothing. A machine that is deallocated loses its temporary disk, which lives on the physical host, not in storage. A machine that is deleted takes its disks with it only if they were set to be deleted with it. A deleted blob is kept for fourteen days, with soft delete on. And deleting the storage account deletes everything in it, which is why accounts are locked down in Course four. The table on the right says which the platform uses. Deals, daily files and the stream go to the lake, as objects, because Spark reads them in parallel. The collateral team's working files go to a file share, because people edit them in place. The runtime's Windows and its logs live on disks, because a machine needs one. And the filed reports are objects that are locked, because nobody may change them. Next, the lake account, and its four zones.

The lake is one storage account with a hierarchical namespace turned on, which is what makes it Data Lake Storage. With it, folders are real: renaming a folder, or giving one a permission, is a single operation instead of one for every file inside. The code at the top is the lake module, now with its four zones as a parameter: landing, bronze, silver and gold. It sets is H n s Enabled to true, and adds a blob service with soft delete for fourteen days, for files and for whole containers, and then one container per zone. The terminal does the same in the storage emulator, against the development account. It creates the four containers, lists them, and uploads the hierarchy file into landing, under a folder for its date, two thousand twenty six, ten, thirteen. The list shows it arrived, five hundred and seven bytes. One difference is worth saying aloud: the emulator has no hierarchical namespace, so the slashes in that name are just characters. On Azure they are folders. The table at the bottom says what each zone is for. Landing holds files exactly as they were delivered, for thirty days, written by the sources and by Data Factory. Bronze holds everything ever received, kept, written by Data Factory and Event Hubs. Silver holds the data cleaned, joined and typed, by Databricks. And gold holds what the risk team reads, the exposures and limits, also built by Databricks. Data only moves forward through the zones, so anything in silver or gold can be rebuilt from bronze. Next, who is allowed to write into landing, and how a source that is not in Azure gets in.

The collateral system is a vendor application in the bank's own data centre, and every evening at nineteen hundred it must drop a file into landing. It has no Azure identity, and the lake's account keys are switched off, so it gets a shared access signature, a S A S: a token that grants exactly the rights and the lifetime it was signed with. The editor shows tools slash drop sas dot py. Drop token signs a token for the landing container with two rights only, create and write, and an expiry. On Azure it is a user delegation S A S, signed with a key the platform asks Entra I D for, valid for at most seven days; the emulator has no Entra I D, so here the emulator's key signs it, and the comment says so. The terminal runs it against the emulator. Writing the file, with a token valid until nineteen thirty, is allowed. Reading it back is refused, four oh three, authorization permission mismatch, because the token has no read right. Listing landing is refused for the same reason: the vendor cannot see what else the bank receives. And yesterday's token is refused outright. The table on the right is who may write where. The collateral system, with a thirty minute token, into landing. Data Factory's managed identity, with a role, into landing and bronze. Databricks, with a role, into bronze through gold. And the risk analysts may only read gold. The list underneath is how the lake decides. Account keys are off, so no key can sign anything. A S A S is signed with a key from Entra I D. Roles are checked first, then a folder's access control list, an A C L, which can open one folder to one identity without a role on the whole container. And every S A S names its rights and its end. Next, what happens when that file arrives twice.

File transfers retry. One evening the collateral delivery times out, the vendor sends it again two minutes later, and the second copy differs: one vessel mortgage has been revalued from six million to five point four. Data Factory had already started reading the first. The editor shows tools slash two deliveries dot py, which plays this out against the emulator three ways. First, plain writes. The first copy is written, the reader notes the file's E tag, a value that changes on every write, and the second copy overwrites it, silently: the last write wins. The reader then asks for the rest of the file only if it is unchanged, and gets four twelve, condition not met. Without that check, it would have read half of one copy and half of the other. Second, write once. The upload is made conditional on the name being new, and the second copy is refused, four oh nine, blob already exists. Third, a lease. The reader takes a sixty second lease, and while it holds it, a writer without the lease is refused, four twelve, lease I D missing, and the reader, with its lease, marks the file as loaded. The table on the right lists the headers behind these. None, and the last write wins. If none match star, only if the name is new. If match an E tag, only if unchanged. And a lease I D, only the lease holder. The list underneath is the rule the landing zone follows. One dated path per delivery. Written once, so a second copy is refused, and the vendor is told. A correction is a new file, never a change to the old one. And a reader pins the E tag it started with. Next, what the lake keeps, and how a file comes back.

Data that is kept forever costs money forever, and most of it is never read again. Storage has access tiers, in the first table on the right. Hot is for data in use. Cool should be kept at least thirty days, cold at least ninety, and both cost less to store and more to read. Archive, kept at least a hundred and eighty days, is offline: reading a file means rehydrating it first, which can take up to fifteen hours. Move or delete a file sooner than its minimum and you pay for the rest anyway. The editor shows templates slash modules slash lifecycle dot bicep: rules the account applies once a day. Landing kept thirty days deletes deliveries older than thirty days. Bronze cools with age moves bronze to cool after thirty days and to cold after ninety. Silver and gold are rebuilt from bronze, so they stay hot, and nothing goes to archive, because Spark cannot read an archived file. The terminal runs tools slash lifecycle plan dot py, a model with hypothetical prices, of the lake after a year at two gigabytes a day. Seven hundred and thirty gigabytes of bronze cost four dollars sixty three a month tiered, against fourteen sixty if all of it stayed hot, plus a dollar twenty for thirty days of landing. Now the part that surprises people: blob versioning does not exist on an account with a hierarchical namespace, and on such an account soft delete keeps deleted files, not overwritten ones. The second table follows from that. A file deleted fourteen days ago or less is undeleted. An overwritten file has no earlier version here, so it is reloaded. A wrong bronze file is reloaded from landing. And if landing's copy is gone too, the source is asked again. That is why landing is written once. Next, the one place where nothing may ever be changed.

Every morning the bank files its large exposures report, and once filed, a report is evidence: the regulator may ask for it years later, and must get exactly what was sent. The map now has its locked reports store. The code at the top is templates slash modules slash reports dot bicep: a separate storage account, so its readers, its redundancy and its policy are its own. Its container, large exposures, carries an immutability policy, write once, read many, for two thousand five hundred and fifty seven days, which is seven years, the bank's retention rule. While the policy applies, no report in the container can be overwritten or deleted, by anyone, administrators included. A new policy starts unlocked, so it can be tested. The script below it, infra slash zero seven lock reports dot sh, reads the policy's E tag and locks it. There is no undo, which the comment says plainly. The table at the bottom is what a locked policy allows. Filing a new report, yes. Overwriting or deleting one, refused for seven years. Extending the retention, allowed, up to five times. Shortening or removing the policy, refused, by anyone. And deleting the container, only once it is empty, which it will not be for seven years. Two things this does not do. It does not stop someone filing a wrong report; it only stops anyone hiding one, so a correction is filed as a new report beside the old. And the emulator has no immutability, so nothing here was run: the template is checked by the Bicep compiler, and the script by the Azure command line's own parser. Next, the two kinds of storage the lake does not cover: a share, and a disk.

The collateral team keeps working spreadsheets that several people edit during the day, and those belong on a file share, not in the lake. The code at the top is templates slash modules slash share dot bicep: a zone redundant storage account with a share called collateral, a hundred gibibytes, over S M B, the protocol Windows uses for shared drives. Its identity setting is Microsoft Entra Kerberos: the team signs in with their own bank accounts, which are synced to Entra I D, so there is no shared password and no storage key on anyone's desktop. Its default share permission is none, so only people given a share role get in. The table in the middle follows a request from a desktop in the bank. The path, port four four five, goes over ExpressRoute to a private endpoint, because public access is disabled, and many internet providers block that port anyway. Who you are is your bank sign in, checked by Kerberos. The share is opened by a role, Storage File Data S M B Share Contributor, given to the collateral team's group. And a folder or file is governed by ordinary Windows permissions underneath. The last table is the runtime machines' disks, from Course six's template. The operating system disk is Premium S S D, locally redundant, one per machine, and it lasts as long as the machine. Each machine also has a temporary disk on its physical host, fine for scratch files and lost when the machine is deallocated. And a snapshot is a copy of a disk at a point in time, kept until it is deleted, which is how a disk is backed up before a risky change. The two machines sit in different zones, so losing one zone loses one disk, not both. Next, what redundancy protects against, and what it does not.

Every storage account keeps several copies of every byte, and the redundancy option chooses where. The table at the top lists them. L R S keeps three copies in one datacentre, which survives a failed disk or rack; development uses it. Z R S keeps three copies across the Region's three availability zones, written at the same time, which survives losing a zone; the lake and the collateral share use it, and Microsoft recommends it for Data Lake Storage. G R S adds a copy in the paired Region, U K West, written a little later. And G Z R S is both: zones here, and a copy in U K West, which the locked reports use, because a regulator's evidence should survive losing London. The list at the bottom left is a failover to U K West. The bank starts it, if U K South is lost. The secondary becomes the primary. Writes that had not been copied yet are lost, and the account's last sync time says from when; with priority replication, block blobs are at most fifteen minutes behind. Afterwards the account is locally redundant until the bank sets it up again. The table on the right is the point of this section: redundancy is not a backup. Every copy copies mistakes too, at once. A file deleted is deleted everywhere, and soft delete undoes it for fourteen days. A file overwritten is overwritten everywhere, and reloading from landing undoes it. If the account itself is deleted, every copy goes with it, and only a backup somewhere else brings it back, which Course thirteen sets up. And a bad job's output is undone by rebuilding from bronze. That completes landing the files. Next, Course eight brings the batches in, with Data Factory.

Data Factory moves data on a schedule or when something happens, and it is built from six parts, in the table on the right. A trigger decides when a pipeline runs. A pipeline is a sequence of activities. An activity is one step: copy, look something up, run a job. A dataset says which data: a table, or a folder of files. A linked service is a connection, and how it signs in. And an integration runtime is the machines that actually move the bytes. The factory keeps all of these in git, one J S O N file per part, in a folder for its kind, which is the explorer's new adf folder. The editor shows adf slash pipeline slash copy tradebook dot json, the first pipeline. Its one activity, Copy Changed Deals, is a Copy activity. Its input is the TradeBook deals dataset, and its output is a Parquet file in bronze. The source is a PostgreSQL query, which is long enough that the editor folds it; the next section prints it in full. The terminal runs tools slash adf parts dot py, which reads the folder and follows the references, the way the factory does. The trigger tr tradebook daily, a tumbling window trigger, starts copy tradebook. Its Copy Changed Deals activity reads ds tradebook deals, through the linked service ls tradebook, on the runtime called ir bank, and writes ds bronze parquet, through ls lake, on the Azure runtime. That one line is the important one: reading TradeBook needs a runtime inside the bank's reach, and writing the lake does not. The list underneath is how these files live: edited in the development factory, saved to git, released by Course six's pipeline, and run in production unchanged. Next, the runtime inside the bank.

TradeBook has no public address, and it never will, so Data Factory cannot reach it from Azure's shared machines. The map now has the integration runtime and Data Factory. The code at the top is templates slash modules slash factory dot bicep. The factory gets its own managed identity, and public network access disabled. Inside it is a self hosted integration runtime called i r bank: software that runs on the bank's own machines, here the two Windows virtual machines from Course six's runtime module. Each machine registers with the runtime using its authentication key, and a runtime can have up to four such nodes, for availability and for capacity. The table in the middle is what running those machines means, because self hosted means the bank runs them. The image is Windows Server twenty twenty two, Azure Edition. The disks are Premium S S D, with the runtime's logs on the operating system disk. The two nodes sit in zones one and three, under one runtime and one key. On the network, they only go out, on port four four three, through the hub firewall, to Data Factory's service. They are patched by Azure Update Manager, one node at a time, so the runtime never stops. And people reach them through Azure Bastion from the hub, because neither has a public I P. The list at the bottom says why this design is the right one. TradeBook has no public address. The runtime reaches it over ExpressRoute. It calls out to Data Factory to ask for work, rather than Data Factory calling in. So nothing inside the bank opens a port inward. Next, the first copy through it: TradeBook's deals.

Copying every deal every night would read the whole of TradeBook every night. The pipeline copies only what changed, one day at a time. Its trigger is a tumbling window trigger: it cuts time into fixed, back to back days, and starts one run per day, handing it the window's start and end, five minutes after the window closes. The query then takes the rows whose updated at falls inside the window. That end is the watermark: everything before it has been copied. There is no Data Factory without a subscription, so the editor shows tools slash copy window dot py, which runs the pipeline's own Copy activity by hand. It reads the query out of the pipeline's J S O N, fills in the window, runs it against TradeBook, here a real PostgreSQL sixteen database standing in for it, and writes the rows as Parquet to the window's folder in bronze, in the storage emulator. The terminal runs it three times. The first load covers everything up to the thirteenth of October: ten deals. Then TradeBook's day happens, from data slash tradebook twenty twenty six ten thirteen dot sql: one insert, one update and one delete. Then the window for the thirteenth: two rows. The table on the right accounts for them. The first load copied ten. The thirteenth copied two: L C twenty forty one, Wide World Importers' new two million letter of credit, and L C nineteen ninety five, amended to one point five. And one change was not seen at all: L C twenty oh seven was deleted, and a deleted row has no updated at to find. The list underneath sums up a watermark by window. The trigger hands each run its window, the query takes rows changed inside it, each window writes its own folder, a failed window reruns alone, and a deleted row changes nothing, because there is no row. Next, files that arrive rather than being fetched.

The hierarchy file lands at eighteen hundred and the collateral file at nineteen hundred, give or take, so a schedule would either wait too long or run too early. Instead, the files start their own pipeline. The map now has Event Grid. When a file is written to the lake, the storage account publishes a blob created event, and Event Grid delivers it to whoever subscribed. The code at the top is adf slash trigger slash tr collateral arrives dot json, a storage event trigger. It subscribes to blob created events, for paths that begin with landing, then the segment blobs, then collateral, and end with dot c s v, and it ignores empty files. It starts load landing file, passing the folder and the file name; the folder Event Grid reports includes the container, so the expression strips landing off the front. The terminal runs tools slash route event dot py, a model of that match, over five events from one evening. The hierarchy file at eighteen hundred starts load landing file for its folder. A collateral file at eighteen fifty eight, put at the top of landing instead of in its folder, starts nothing, and the support team would hear about it from the next section's checks. The real collateral file at nineteen hundred starts load landing file. An empty placeholder for tomorrow is ignored. And the deals Parquet file in bronze starts nothing, because no trigger watches bronze. The list at the bottom is what the trigger needs. Event Grid registered on the subscription. The lake letting Event Grid through, even though it is private. Whoever publishes the trigger allowed to manage the lake's events. And a file written whole, so there is one event per completed file. Next, what load landing file checks before it copies anything.

A file from another team is an agreement, whether anyone wrote it down or not, and this one is written down: contracts slash hierarchy dot json lists the hierarchy file's columns, in order, a pattern for each column's values, and its key, the counterparty I D, agreed with the client data team on the first of September. Load landing file checks the columns before it copies anything, and fails the run if they differ. The editor shows tools slash check contract dot py, the full check, values included, which runs locally here and in Databricks later. It finds the contract from the file's name, compares the header with the agreed columns, lists any missing and any unexpected, then checks every value against its column's pattern, and finally that the key is unique. The terminal checks two days' files. The thirteenth's agrees: five columns, nine rows. The fourteenth's is refused. The counterparty I D column is missing, because the source renamed it c p t y I D. There are two unexpected columns, that renamed one and a new one called L E I, a legal entity identifier. And all nine country codes break the pattern, because the source switched from two letter codes, G B, to three letter codes, G B R. The table on the right lines those changes up, agreed against delivered. Any one of them would have broken the exposure numbers quietly: a join on counterparty I D finds nothing, and a group's exposure drops to zero. The list underneath is the rule. The contract is written down: columns, order, formats and key. A file that breaks it is refused whole, never half loaded. The source is told the same evening. A change is agreed first, and becomes a new version of the contract. And it is never fixed silently in the pipeline. Next, checking that the lake agrees with TradeBook.

Every copy can go wrong in a way that raises no error, so every night the lake is reconciled with its source. The editor shows tools slash reconcile dot py. It asks TradeBook, still the local PostgreSQL sixteen database, for every deal and its amount. It then reads every daily window in bronze, from the storage emulator, and keeps each deal at its latest version. It counts and sums both sides, and lists every deal that differs, one by one, never as a single net figure. The terminal shows the result after the thirteenth. TradeBook has ten deals worth twenty seven point eight million. The lake has eleven, worth twenty eight point seven. The difference is one deal: L C twenty oh seven, absent from TradeBook and still in the lake at nought point nine million. It was deleted on the thirteenth, and a query by window cannot see a row that no longer exists. Left alone, Contoso Freight would carry a cancelled letter of credit in tomorrow's exposure. The table on the right compares the two ways to copy changes. Copying by window reads the rows that changed, cannot see deletes, puts one query a day on TradeBook, and is a day behind. Change data capture reads the database's own log of inserts, updates and deletes, so it sees deletes, needs a replication slot on TradeBook, and is minutes behind. The bank's database team must agree to that slot, so for now the platform keeps the daily copy and reconciles it, and the stream in Course nine is where capture by log arrives. The list underneath is the nightly rule: count and sum on both sides, list every deal that differs, and stop the report run when anything does. Next, what happens when a run fails halfway and is run again.

Pipelines fail halfway: the runtime loses its connection to TradeBook after writing part of a window, and the retry runs the whole window again. Whether that doubles the data depends only on how the load writes. The editor shows tools slash rerun window dot py, which plays it out in the storage emulator with two parts of the thirteenth's window: the files are real, and the failure is raised on purpose. Its run function writes each part, and stops after the first if told to fail. In append mode, each run names its files after its run I D, so nothing is ever overwritten. In replace mode, the window has one folder and fixed file names. Each mode runs twice: first failing after part one, then succeeding. The terminal shows the difference. Append ends with three files and three rows, for a window that has two: the failed run's part one is still there beside the retry's. Replace ends with two files and two rows, because the retry wrote the same names again. That property, running twice leaves the same result as once, is called idempotent. The table on the right applies it. Appending a file per run duplicates on a rerun. One folder per window replaces. Inserting into a table duplicates. Merging on the key replaces. The platform's loads are all of the second kind. The list underneath is how the pipeline fails well. The copy retries twice, five minutes apart. A failed window is rerun alone, from the trigger's run history. The next window waits, because the trigger runs one window at a time. And everything downstream reads only finished windows. Next, the last piece: how the pipelines sign in, without a single password in the factory.

The factory signs in to three things: the lake, Key Vault and TradeBook. The editor shows adf slash linked service slash ls tradebook dot json, the connection to TradeBook. It names the server, the port, the database, a user called a d f reader with read access only, and certificate checking on the T L S connection. Its password is not in the file: it is an Azure Key Vault secret reference, to the secret tradebook a d f reader, read through the linked service ls keyvault. And it connects via i r bank, the runtime inside the bank. The terminal runs tools slash adf parts dot py with credentials, which lists how each connection signs in. The vault and the lake: the factory's own managed identity, with no secret at all. TradeBook: a user and a Key Vault secret, because PostgreSQL in the bank does not know Entra I D. The table on the right is what the factory's identity holds, from templates slash modules slash factory dot bicep, which now assigns its roles. Key Vault Secrets User on the production vault, and Storage Blob Data Contributor on landing and on bronze, and nothing on silver or gold, which only Databricks writes. One problem follows: the templates now assign roles, and the deployment identity is a Contributor, which cannot. So infra slash zero eight deploy can assign dot sh gives it Role Based Access Control Administrator, with a condition: it may assign these two roles and no others, never Owner. The list at the bottom sums it up. The lake, by the factory's own identity. TradeBook, by a password kept in Key Vault, rotated there with nothing redeployed. The role assignments live in factory dot bicep. And the deployer may grant these two roles only. That completes the batches. Next, Course nine brings the stream in.

Course eight's batches bring in yesterday, reconciled and complete, in time for the seven o'clock report. Some things cannot wait for the night. The table at the top follows Wide World Group through one day, with a limit of ten million and a net exposure of eight point four when the report goes out. At nine o'clock, sterling moves one per cent, and a deal priced in sterling is worth more in dollars. The batch sees that at five past midnight; a stream sees it two seconds later. At half past three, a new two million letter of credit is booked, and net exposure becomes ten point four. The batch sees it after midnight again. And at fifteen thirty one, the group is over its limit, and nobody knows: with only the batch, the seven o'clock report is the first anyone hears of it. With a stream, an alert goes out at fifteen thirty and five seconds; Course twelve builds that alert. The table at the bottom left compares the two ways in. A batch moves a file, or a day's window, and takes hours; a stream moves one event, and takes seconds. The batch is right for the report of record; the stream for what changed just now. And the batch is complete, because it is reconciled every night, while the stream is complete eventually, and the batch checks it. The list on the right names the platform's two streams. f x rates carries every exchange rate change, all day. Deal events carries every deal being booked, amended, issued and closed. Both feed the intraday exposure, and the seven o'clock report still comes from the batch. Next, the service that carries them: Event Hubs.

The map now has Event Hubs. The code at the top is templates slash modules slash streaming dot bicep. It creates one namespace on the Standard tier, which is the lowest tier with the Kafka endpoint, with two throughput units of capacity, auto inflate allowed up to four, public network access disabled, and local authentication disabled, so no shared access key can ever be used: Entra I D only. Inside it are two event hubs, f x rates and deal events, each with four partitions, keeping events for one day, and each with a consumer group for the intraday exposure. The terminal runs tools slash send events dot py against the Event Hubs emulator, and shows where each event landed. f x rates has four partitions. G B P U S D goes to partition three, E U R U S D to one, S G D U S D to two, and the second G B P U S D goes to partition three again, as number one after number nought. That is the partition key at work: the same key, the same partition, so one currency pair's rates stay in the order they were sent. Deal events are keyed by the deal, so all of L C twenty forty one's events stay in order too; here L C nineteen ninety five happens to share its partition. Across partitions there is no order at all. The table at the bottom translates. A namespace is the service, with one address, which Kafka calls a cluster. An event hub is one stream, like f x rates, which Kafka calls a topic. A partition is an ordered lane inside it. A partition key picks the lane. And a consumer group is one reader's own position in the stream. Next, the bank's existing Kafka producer, moved onto this namespace.

The bank already has a producer that publishes market data to its own Kafka cluster, and it should not need rewriting. The editor shows feeds slash market producer dot py, the bank's code. It reads a properties file, makes a Kafka producer from it, and publishes each rate in data slash f x twenty twenty six ten thirteen dot c s v to the topic f x rates, keyed by currency pair. Nothing in it names a cluster. The table on the right is the whole migration: the difference between feeds slash bank dot properties and feeds slash azure dot properties. The bootstrap server becomes the namespace's address, on port nine oh nine three. The security protocol stays S A S L over S S L. The mechanism becomes O AUTH BEARER, and the credential becomes an Entra I D token for the producer's app registration, because the namespace accepts no keys. And the code is unchanged. The terminal runs the same producer against the emulator, using feeds slash emulator dot properties, which speaks plain text on port nine oh nine two with the emulator's fixed development key. Six rates are delivered, each with its partition and offset, and the three G B P U S D rates share partition one, at offsets nought, one and two. Notice that the previous section's G B P U S D went to partition three. A Kafka client chooses the partition itself, by hashing the key its own way, while the Event Hubs S D K lets the service choose. Both keep a key together, but not in the same place, so each hub is written one way only: f x rates by Kafka, deal events by the S D K. The list underneath sums up the move: the namespace is the cluster, each hub is a topic, and there is no broker to run, patch or grow. Next, reading the stream, and carrying on after a restart.

A stream is read, not emptied: the events stay in the hub for a day, and each reader keeps its own place. The editor shows tools slash intraday reader dot py. It reads deal events as the consumer group exposure intraday, and keeps its checkpoints in a blob container called checkpoints, in the lake's storage account. For each event, it handles it, and then updates its checkpoint: the offset and sequence number it reached in that partition. If there is no checkpoint yet, it starts from the oldest event the hub still has. The terminal runs it against the emulators. The first run reads three events, all in partition nought: L C twenty forty one booked, L C nineteen ninety five amended, and L C twenty forty one issued, and saves its checkpoint. Then tools slash deal event dot py publishes one new event, L C twenty forty two booked. The second run reads only that one, from partition two, because everything before it was already checkpointed. The table on the right lists the readers of deal events. Exposure intraday reads for the intraday exposure. The default group is left unused. And Capture, in the next section, needs no group at all. The list underneath is what checkpoints mean. They are kept per group and per partition, in blob storage. They are written after an event is handled. A restart carries on from the last one. But a crash between handling an event and checkpointing it means that event comes again after the restart. So the handling must be safe to repeat: recalculating a deal's exposure twice gives the same answer, while sending an alert twice does not, which is why alerts go through Service Bus, later in this course. Next, keeping every event, with no reader at all.

Event Hubs keeps events for a day, and the platform needs them for years: to replay a day, to reconcile the stream against the batch, and to answer the auditors. Event Hubs Capture writes every event to the lake, with no reader to run. The code at the top is the streaming module with Capture added. A capture setting, shared by both hubs, is enabled, writes Avro files, closes a file every three hundred seconds or every three hundred megabytes, whichever comes first, and skips windows with no events. Its destination is the bronze container, and it writes as the namespace's own managed identity, which the namespace now has. The file names follow a path of namespace, hub, partition, then year, month, day, hour, minute and second. At the bottom of the module, a role assignment gives that identity Storage Blob Data Contributor on bronze, one of the two roles the deployment identity is allowed to grant. The table in the middle reads one such path. The namespace and hub, e v h w g risk prod slash deal events. The partition, two. The window, to the second: the thirteenth of October, fourteen twenty five. And the file, Avro, holding each event's body, offset and enqueued time. The emulator has no Capture, so nothing here was run: the module is checked by the Bicep compiler. The list at the bottom is why the platform captures as well as reads. The hub keeps events a day, and bronze keeps them. There is nothing to run, so no reader and no checkpoints. Databricks can replay any day from bronze. And the nightly batch reconciles against it. Next, a step back: four services that move messages, and which job each one fits.

Azure has four services that move a message, and they are easy to mix up, because each can be bent into doing another's job. Queue Storage is a simple queue inside a storage account: small messages, up to sixty four kilobytes, no ordering, no sessions, cheap, for a simple list of work. Service Bus is a broker for commands and business messages: queues and topics, sessions that keep one key's messages in order, duplicates dropped, dead letters kept aside, and each message settled exactly once by whoever handles it. Event Grid pushes notices that something happened, like a file arrived or a machine stopped, to whoever subscribed, filtered, retried and finally dead lettered; it is not for a stream of data. Event Hubs is a log of events, taking millions a second, keeping them a day or more so they can be replayed, read by many readers at their own positions, in order only within a partition. The table at the bottom gives each its job on the platform. A file landed, so load it: Event Grid, because it is a notice, pushed, as Course eight set up. Every exchange rate and every deal event: Event Hubs, because it is a stream, with several readers and replay. A deal's steps, in order, each handled once: Service Bus, because of sessions, duplicate detection and dead letters. And an over the limit alert that someone must act on: Service Bus too, because it must not be lost or doubled; Course twelve sends it. Next, Service Bus for the deal's steps.

A letter of credit goes through steps: booked, documents checked, issued. Each must be handled once, in order, and a step that cannot be handled must not block the others or vanish. The map now has Service Bus, and templates slash modules slash messaging dot bicep creates its deal steps queue. The editor shows tools slash deal steps dot py, run against the Service Bus emulator. It sends six messages, each with the deal as its session I D and a message I D made of the deal and the step. One is a retry by the sender, a second L C twenty forty one issued, and one, L C twenty forty two issued, names no beneficiary, so it cannot be handled. A reader then takes each deal's session in turn, and either completes a message or abandons it. The terminal shows the result. Six messages were sent. L C twenty forty one's three steps were completed in order, booked, documents checked, issued, and the repeat of issued never arrived: duplicate detection dropped it, because a message with the same I D had been seen within the window. L C twenty forty two booked was completed. Its issued step was abandoned three times, delivery one, two and three, and then moved to the dead letter queue, with the reason max delivery count exceeded. The table on the right is the queue's settings, each with its purpose: a session per deal keeps a deal's steps in order; duplicate detection for ten minutes drops a resent step; a thirty second lock frees a message again if its reader crashes; and after three deliveries, a message goes to the dead letters. The emulator allows only five minutes and an hour where the template asks ten minutes and a day, so its configuration says so. The list underneath is how a message is settled, and the rule that someone reads the dead letters every day. Next, what every stream reader must expect.

A stream breaks three assumptions that a batch lets you keep. The editor shows tools slash stream rules dot py, a plain Python model of all three, and the terminal runs it. First, throttling. On the Standard tier, one throughput unit takes in up to a thousand events a second, or a megabyte. At the eight o'clock market open, rates arrive at two thousand six hundred a second for five seconds. With two units, six hundred a second are refused, with an error called server busy, the producer backs off and retries, and everything is in by seven seconds. With three units, nothing is refused, and it is in by five. Auto inflate adds units when that happens, up to four, but never takes them away again, so somebody must. Second, late events. Rates are counted in the minute they happened, which is event time, not the time they reached the hub. The fourteen hundred minute stays open for ten seconds after it ends. G B P U S D, from fourteen hundred and fifty eight seconds, arrived a second later and is counted. E U R U S D arrived nine seconds late and is still counted. S G D U S D arrived twenty four seconds late, too late, so it becomes a correction to that minute. Third, duplicates. A sender that retries can deliver an event twice: four deal events received, three kept, one duplicate dropped by its event I D. The table on the right is one throughput unit: in, a megabyte or a thousand events a second; out, two megabytes or four thousand and ninety six events; over it, server busy, retry and back off; and auto inflate, up to four, never down. The list underneath is what a stream does not promise: order across partitions, arrival in the order things happened, or each event exactly once. So: key by deal, count by event time, and drop repeats by event I D. That completes the stream. Next, Course ten transforms it all in Databricks.

Databricks is where the platform's Spark jobs turn bronze into silver and gold, and to Azure it is first of all a resource, deployed like any other. The map now has Databricks. The code at the top is templates slash modules slash databricks dot bicep. An access connector comes first: a small Azure resource whose only job is to hold a managed identity, which the next section puts to work. Then the workspace itself, d b w w g risk prod, on the Premium tier, which private link and Unity Catalog's controls need. It names a managed resource group, sets public network access to disabled, and its parameters place it in the spoke's virtual network, in the two Databricks subnets from Course five, with no public I P addresses on its machines. The first table is what deploying it creates. The workspace belongs to the bank. The managed resource group belongs to Databricks, and is locked so that nobody else can change it. Inside it is the workspace's own storage, and, while clusters run, their virtual machines: Databricks creates them, and the bank pays for them. And the access connector belongs to the bank. The second table draws the line between this course and the Databricks data engineering course. Here: the workspace, its network and its identities; the lake's roles and Key Vault; and the virtual machines, quotas and the bill. There: notebooks, Spark and Delta; Unity Catalog's grants; and jobs, Auto Loader and Lakeflow. This course stops at the workspace's front door, with everything the workspace needs from Azure in place. Next, how the workspace sits in the network.

Databricks clusters run in the bank's own network, which is called V Net injection. Each cluster node gets two addresses, one in the host subnet and one in the container subnet, both delegated to Databricks in Course five; the A P I still calls them the public and private subnets. The code at the top is the network module's change for it: Databricks needs a network security group on both subnets, so the module now creates n s g snet d b x and attaches it to any subnet delegated to Databricks. Databricks manages that group's rules itself. The terminal runs tools slash d b x capacity dot py, a model of whether the clusters fit. Each subnet is a slash twenty six, with fifty nine usable addresses. The overnight job needs seventeen nodes, sixteen workers and a driver, at night. By day, the intraday job needs three and three engineers' clusters fifteen. The busiest moment is eighteen nodes at once, which leaves forty one addresses spare. If the subnets were too small, clusters would fail to start, and subnets are hard to grow once in use, which is why Course five sized them for the peak. The table at the bottom is the three paths in and out, all private. An engineer reaches the workspace through front end private link, via the hub. A cluster reaches Databricks' control plane through back end private link, and only ever connects outwards: that is secure cluster connectivity. A cluster reaches the lake through the private endpoints in snet p e. And from the internet to a cluster there is nothing at all: no public I P, no open port. Next, how a cluster is allowed to read the lake.

A Spark job needs to read bronze and write silver and gold, and nobody should hand it a key. The editor shows the Databricks module's two halves that make that work. The access connector has a system assigned managed identity. A role assignment gives that identity Storage Blob Data Contributor on the lake, one of the two roles the deployment identity may grant. The terminal compiles the module and lists what it declares: the access connector, the workspace, a private endpoint for the workspace, which the clusters use to reach the control plane, and the role assignment, after the access connector. The table on the right follows the chain from that Azure role to a person reading a file. The connector's identity, in Azure, from this module. Storage Blob Data Contributor, in Azure, on the lake. Then, inside Databricks, a storage credential made from the connector; an external location, which is a path in the lake using that credential; and a grant on that location, such as read files, to a group. The last three are Unity Catalog, which the Databricks course teaches; this course's part is that only one identity in Azure ever holds a role on the lake. The list underneath says why that matters. Only the connector holds a lake role. There are no keys and no shared access signatures in any notebook. Who reads what is decided by Unity Catalog grants, which are visible in one place. And taking someone's access away is one revoke. Next, the secrets Databricks still needs, and the people who use it.

Some jobs still need a password, such as a read only login to TradeBook for a nightly check, and a notebook must never contain one. Databricks reads secrets through a secret scope, and a scope can be backed by Azure Key Vault. There is a catch, in the first table on the right. The platform's vault, k v w g risk prod, uses Azure roles for its permissions, and a Key Vault backed scope supports only the older access policy model. So Databricks gets its own small vault, k v w g d b x prod, created by templates slash modules slash d b x vault dot bicep. It uses access policies, holds only the secrets Databricks jobs need, and lets trusted Microsoft services through its firewall, because Databricks reads it from its control plane. The editor shows infra slash ten secret scope dot sh. It looks up the vault's I D, then, with the Databricks command line rather than the Azure one, creates a scope called risk k v backed by that vault, which also gives Databricks' own application permission to get and list its secrets. It then grants read on the scope to the Risk Data Engineers group, and to nobody else. The terminal runs tools slash secret read dot py, a model of who can read the TradeBook password. Priya, in Risk Data Engineers, reads it, and if a notebook prints it, Databricks shows redacted. Omar, in Risk Analysts, is refused: no read on risk k v. Sam, in Credit Officers, cannot even sign in, because that group was never added to the workspace. The list underneath is how people get in: Entra groups, synced into Databricks, never local users; a group is added to the workspace; and the scope's access list decides who reads which secret. Next, the machines Databricks runs on, and what they do to the Azure bill.

Every Databricks cluster node is an Azure virtual machine in the bank's own subscription, so it uses the subscription's quotas and appears on its bill. The table on the right is the choice for the overnight job: Standard D four d s version five machines, four virtual C P Us and sixteen gibibytes each, from a family whose quota in the subscription is a hundred virtual C P Us, an assumed figure the platform team requested. Workers run on Spot, and the driver always on demand. The editor shows policies slash databricks slash overnight job dot json, a cluster policy: rules every cluster created under it must follow. The machine type is allowed only from a list of one. Workers are at most sixteen. Availability is fixed at Spot with fallback to Azure on demand. The first node, the driver, is always on demand. And two tags are fixed, app and env, so every cluster's cost can be traced. The terminal runs tools slash compute plan dot py, a model with hypothetical prices. The overnight job needs sixty eight virtual C P Us, which fits the quota of a hundred; by day, the intraday job and three engineers need seventy two. One night's virtual machines cost six dollars eighty all on demand, and two dollars thirty two with the workers on Spot, at a hypothetical six cents an hour against twenty. Spot machines are spare capacity that Azure can take back at any moment; when it does, the policy falls back to on demand, and the job takes longer rather than failing. The list underneath is what the policy prevents: a bigger machine nobody budgeted for, more than sixteen workers, a driver evicted in the middle of a run, and a cluster without its cost tags. Next, who starts the job each night.

The exposure job must run after TradeBook's copy has finished, and never before. Databricks has its own scheduler, and Data Factory has its triggers, so something has to own the order. The code on the right is adf slash pipeline slash nightly dot json, the night's pipeline. Its first activity runs copy tradebook, the pipeline from Course eight, and waits for it to complete. Its second, Build Exposure, is a Databricks Job activity. It depends on the copy succeeding, connects through a new linked service, l s databricks, which signs in as the factory's own managed identity, retries once after ten minutes, and runs an existing Databricks job by its I D, passing the business date. The tumbling window trigger from Course eight now starts nightly instead of the copy alone. For that sign in to work, the factory's identity is added to the workspace, with permission to run that one job. The table at the bottom compares the two ways to start it. Data Factory waits for the TradeBook copy and for files; Databricks' scheduler waits for a time, a file arriving or a table changing. Data Factory sees the whole night, sources included; Databricks sees only Databricks. So the platform uses Data Factory for the night, where the order spans both, and Databricks' own scheduler for the intraday job that reads the stream, which needs nothing outside Databricks. One rule follows: each job has exactly one owner that starts it, or it runs twice. Next, what one night of all this costs.

Databricks sends two bills for every node hour, and both are needed to know what a night costs. The first table on the right names them. The virtual machine, billed by Azure, at the hypothetical rate card's twenty cents an hour, or six cents on Spot. And D B Us, Databricks Units, billed for the software: a number of units per node hour for each machine size, here an assumed nought point seven five, at a hypothetical fifteen cents each. Disks and network are left out. The editor shows tools slash night cost dot py, which adds them up for the two jobs, and the terminal shows the answer. The overnight job runs sixteen workers and a driver for two hours: thirty four node hours. Its machines cost two dollars thirty two with Spot workers, its D B Us three dollars eighty two, so six dollars fourteen a run, and a hundred and eighty four thirty five over thirty nights. The intraday job runs two workers and a driver for ten hours: thirty node hours, all on demand. Its machines cost six dollars, its D B Us three thirty eight, nine thirty eight a run, two hundred and six twenty five over twenty two working days. The total is three hundred and ninety dollars sixty a month, hypothetically. Course one's ten dollars forty a day counted only the workers' machines. The list underneath is what the numbers say. The intraday job costs more than the night, because it runs ten hours. Spot cut the night's machines by two thirds. D B Us do not fall with Spot. And tags on every cluster let the bill be split by job. That completes Databricks' Azure side. Next, Course eleven serves the results.

Gold holds the answers; this course puts them where each reader can use them, and each reader asks something different. The table at the top lists three readers. The exposure A P I serves the dealers: it is asked for Wide World's headroom, now, hundreds of times a second, which needs one row by key, in milliseconds. It is also asked to reserve one million of that headroom for a deal in progress, a few times a minute, which needs a transaction that cannot overbook. The risk team, in Power B I, asks for exposure by group, by country and by day, all day long, which needs S Q L: joins, sums and history. And the regulator receives the seven o'clock large exposures file once a day, which must be complete, dated and unchangeable. One store cannot do all of that well, so the table at the bottom left gives each ask its own. The risk mart, on PostgreSQL, answers headroom, reservations and the reports, because it has transactions and S Q L. The group lookup, on Cosmos D B, answers a group and its members, by one key, at any scale. A cache, on Redis, answers the dashboard's headroom, fast, but possibly seconds old. And Course seven's locked reports keep the regulator's file, which nobody can change. The list on the right is the rule that holds them together. A decision, such as approving a reservation, reads the mart, never the cache. Every copy says how old it may be. And gold stays the source: every one of these stores can be reloaded from it. Next, which relational database the mart should be.

Azure offers four ways to run a relational database, and the table at the top compares them. Azure S Q L Database runs the S Q L Server engine as a managed service: the bank manages only its data, high availability across zones is built in, and it can be restored to any point in time. S Q L Managed Instance is a whole S Q L Server instance, managed, for moving an existing instance with its agent jobs and cross database queries. S Q L Server on a virtual machine is the full product, for whatever needs the operating system, but then the bank patches it, backs it up and builds its own high availability. And Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server runs community PostgreSQL as a managed service, with a zone redundant standby and point in time restore. The table at the bottom left is why the mart uses PostgreSQL flexible server. TradeBook is already PostgreSQL, so the bank needs one skill set, not two. Reservations need serializable transactions, which PostgreSQL does well. A zone redundant standby and point in time restore are built in. Nothing in the mart needs S Q L Agent or instance level features, which rules out Managed Instance. And nothing needs the operating system, which rules out a virtual machine. The list on the right is what would change the answer. An existing S Q L Server estate, with its skills and licences, would point to Azure S Q L. A vendor product that depends on S Q L Agent would need Managed Instance. And a product that needs the operating system itself would need a virtual machine. Next, the mart itself.

The map now has the risk mart. The code at the top is templates slash modules slash mart dot bicep: a PostgreSQL sixteen flexible server called p s q l w g riskmart prod. Its tier is General Purpose with two virtual cores, a Standard D two d s version five. It runs in zone one, with zone redundant high availability: a standby in zone three, kept in step with every commit, which takes over automatically if zone one is lost. It keeps fourteen days of backups, copied to U K West. Sign in is Entra I D only, with password authentication disabled, so there is no password to leak. Public network access is off, and a private endpoint in snet p e is the only way in, which Course five's security group already allows from the A P I's subnet on port five four three two. The terminal builds the mart's schema on a real PostgreSQL sixteen, running locally, from s q l slash mart dot s q l: groups with their limits, the exposure loaded from gold, reservations, and a headroom view. Wide World Group has a limit of ten, net exposure of eight point four, nothing reserved, and headroom of one point six. Tailspin Traders has the least, nought point seven. The table at the bottom is what happens when something breaks. If zone one is lost, the standby in zone three takes over. If a bad load runs at ten past six, the mart is restored to six o'clock, and restoring always creates a new server, which the A P I is then pointed at. And if U K South is lost entirely, a server is restored from the backup copy in U K West. Next, what happens when two dealers reserve the same headroom at once.

Two dealers, at the same moment, each want to reserve one million of Wide World's headroom for a new letter of credit. There is one point six left, enough for one of them, not both. The editor shows tools slash reserve headroom dot py, which runs both transactions against the mart on PostgreSQL sixteen, stepping them in the same interleaved order every time. Each transaction checks the headroom, then inserts its reservation. The terminal shows the run twice. First at read committed, PostgreSQL's default. A sees one point six, B sees one point six: both enough. A holds one million and commits. B holds one million and commits. The headroom is now minus nought point four: the limit was broken, by two transactions that each did the right thing. Then at serializable. Both see one point six again, and A commits. But when B tries to commit, PostgreSQL refuses it: could not serialize. It has noticed that B's decision rested on a reading that A's commit made false. B rechecks and finds nought point six, which is too little, so its dealer is told no. The headroom is nought point six, as it should be. The table on the right sums up the options. Read committed lets both commit. Serializable refuses one, with error code four oh oh oh one. A lock, select for update on the group's row, makes one wait and then see nought point six. The list underneath is the mart's rule for money. Check and hold in one transaction. Use serializable for every reservation. Retry a four oh oh oh one from the check, never from the insert. And let the database refuse, not the A P I. Next, connecting to the mart, and which failures are safe to retry.

Networks fail at the worst moment: a reservation commits, and the reply never reaches the A P I. The A P I sees an error, and cannot tell whether the reservation happened. The editor shows tools slash retry safely dot py, run against the mart on PostgreSQL sixteen, with that lost reply staged. Its reserve function inserts a reservation of half a million in one of two ways. Without a key, every attempt gets a new I D. With a key, the request's own I D, a second attempt finds the first and does nothing, because of on conflict do nothing. The main loop makes each reservation twice: the first attempt commits and its reply is lost, so the A P I retries. The terminal shows the difference. Without a key, two reservations, one million held for one deal of half a million. With the key, one reservation, half a million held. The table on the right says what is safe to retry. Reading headroom, always. Reserving with a key, yes, and it happens once. Reserving without a key, no, because it holds twice. A serialization failure or a timeout, retry, with a growing wait between attempts. And a check constraint violation, never: that is an answer, not a fault. The list underneath is how the A P I connects at all. It signs in as its own managed identity, and its password is an Entra I D token, valid for about an hour, which the connection pool must renew. Each instance of the A P I keeps a pool: ten instances with ten connections each is a hundred. And every pool counts against the server's maximum number of connections, which depends on its size, so pools are sized on purpose. Next, the other store: a lookup by group.

The A P I is asked, many times a second, which group a counterparty belongs to and who else is in it. That is a lookup by key, and Cosmos D B is built for it. The editor shows tools slash group lookup dot py, run against the Cosmos D B emulator. It creates a container called groups whose partition key is slash group I D, so every item for one group lives together, in one logical partition. It loads the nine counterparties and the five groups from the hierarchy file. Then three reads. A point read, by an item's I D and its partition key, fetches Wide World Group directly. A query with the partition key, for Wide World's members, stays inside one partition: C one oh one and C one oh two. And a query by counterparty I D alone, without the key, has to ask every partition before it finds that C five oh two is in Northwind Group. The emulator reports a flat cost for everything, so the first table on the right takes the costs from the documentation. A point read of a one kilobyte item costs one request unit. A query with the key costs a few, in one partition. A query without it costs a few times every partition. The second table is the warning in this design: one giant group is a hot partition. Throughput is divided evenly across physical partitions, so with four thousand request units a second over four partitions, each gets a thousand. Today, twelve hundred lookups a second put three hundred on the busiest. If lookups grow to three thousand and forty per cent are for one group, that group's partition needs twelve hundred, and is throttled, while the container as a whole is below its limit. Next, keeping two editors and several items consistent.

Cosmos D B has two kinds of consistency to think about: what a reader may see, and what happens when two writers collide. The first table on the right lists the five consistency levels, strongest first. Strong: always the latest write. Bounded staleness: at most a set number of versions or seconds behind. Session, the account's setting here: a client always sees its own writes, in order. Consistent prefix: possibly old, but never out of order. And eventual: anything, eventually. With one Region they behave alike; the differences appear with several. The editor shows tools slash group update dot py, against the emulator. Two analysts open Wide World Group at the same moment. Each saves a note with the item's E tag as a condition, if match. A's note, on watch, is saved. B's note, limit review, is refused with four twelve, because the item changed since B read it: B must reread and decide again, instead of silently overwriting A. Then a transactional batch adds a new counterparty, C one oh three, and updates the group's member count to three, together, and both are applied. The same batch again, adding C one oh one, which already exists, fails with four oh nine, and neither change is applied: the member count stays three, not four. The list underneath gives the batch's limits: one partition key, up to a hundred operations, all applied or none. So moving a counterparty from one group to another, which touches two partition keys, cannot be one batch, and needs its own design: in this platform, the nightly reload from gold. Next, a cache in front of the mart.

The dashboard asks for headroom far more often than it changes, so a cache sits in front of the mart, on Azure Managed Redis, signed in with Entra I D and no access keys. A cache answers fast because it answers from a copy, and a copy can be old. The editor shows tools slash cache headroom dot py, a plain Python model of cache aside: read the cache; on a miss, read the mart and keep the answer for sixty seconds. At ten seconds, a dealer reserves one million of Wide World's one point six. The terminal shows what the dashboard displays every ten seconds. With expiry alone, it shows one point six until the sixty second copy expires, fifty seconds after the headroom had fallen to nought point six. With the writer also deleting the cached copy when it commits, the dashboard shows nought point six from ten seconds on. Deleting on write narrows the gap but cannot close it completely, because a reader can refill the cache with the old value between the write and the delete, so the time to live stays as a backstop. The table on the right decides how stale is too stale, use by use. A dashboard tile can be up to sixty seconds old. A dealer's screen reads the cache, deleted on write. Reserving headroom reads the mart, always, as the last two sections showed. And the seven o'clock report comes from gold, never from a cache. The list underneath is the cache's rules: every entry has a time to live, a write deletes what it changed, a decision never reads the cache, and if the cache is down, the mart answers, more slowly. The dealers' screens ask one service for headroom and reservations: the exposure A P I. The editor shows app slash server dot p y, the part that matters, the reserve function. Otherwise it inserts the reservation with on conflict do nothing, so a retried request holds nothing twice, and returns two oh one with the headroom that remains. If PostgreSQL reports a serialization failure, it tries again, up to three times. That is everything Course eleven taught, in one function. And it does not write log files: it prints one line per request to its output, which App Service collects. Next, running it on App Service.

Next, those settings, and why none of them is a secret.

An application's settings are where secrets usually leak: into a template, a repository, a screenshot. The editor shows the app's settings in app dot bicep. AZURE CLIENT I D tells the A P I which of its identities to sign in as. And the last setting, the limits service key, is not a value at all: it is a Key Vault reference, naming the vault and a secret called limits key. None is a secret written into the template, which the check would flag in capitals. And references are read as the app's identity. The table on the right explains why only one secret is left. The risk mart, the group lookup and the cache all accept Entra I D tokens, so the A P I signs in to each as its own identity, and there is nothing to store. Only the bank's limits system, on premises, accepts nothing but an A P I key, so that key lives in Key Vault, and app slash limits dot p y reads it from the environment. And when the secret is rotated in Key Vault, App Service picks up the new value without a redeployment. Next, releasing a new version without anyone noticing.

A new release must not make the dealers' screens stall, and a bad one must be undone in seconds. The script at the top is infra slash twelve release dot sh. It zips the app folder and deploys it, not to production, but to the staging slot: a second, live copy of the app with its own address, running on the same plan. It then checks the staging slot's state. And it swaps staging into production. The swap first warms the production instances with the new code, then switches traffic, so nobody meets a cold start. The old release is now in staging, still warm, so rolling back is the same swap again. The first table is scaling, which App Service does two ways. Scaling up changes the plan's size, from P one v three to P two v three, by hand and rarely. Scaling out changes the number of instances, and autoscale does it: from three to ten, adding an instance when average C P U stays above seventy per cent for ten minutes, and removing one when it falls below thirty, with ten minutes' cooldown so it does not flap. Three is the floor, one per zone. The second table is health and logs. The health check path, slash health, takes an instance that keeps failing out of the load balancer's rotation. Standard output, the A P I's one line per request, is collected by App Service, and Course thirteen sends it on to Log Analytics. The staging slot warms before the swap. And swapping again is the rollback. Next, a step back: other places the same A P I could have run.

The exposure A P I could have run in six places, and the table at the top compares them by what the bank must run itself. On a virtual machine, the bank runs the operating system, its patches and the web server, and scales by adding machines by hand: all the work, for nothing the A P I needs. On a scale set, the bank runs an operating system image and its updates, and scales by whole machines; that is only worth it for software that needs the operating system. On App Service, the choice, the bank runs only its code, and instances scale automatically, with slots and zones built in. On Container Apps, the bank runs a container image, and replicas scale, even to zero; it would fit equally well if the A P I were packaged as a container. On A K S, managed Kubernetes, the bank runs clusters, node pools and their upgrades: one A P I is not a reason to run a platform. And on Functions, the bank runs a function, triggered by events and billed per execution, which suits the breach alert, not an A P I that is always busy. The table at the bottom left shows where each part of the platform runs, and why. The exposure A P I on App Service, because it is always on and needs slots. The breach alert on Functions, because it is an event, now and then. The breach workflow on Durable Functions, because it waits half an hour for a person. The report filer as a Container Apps job, because it runs once a day, as a container. And the integration runtime on virtual machines, because it is Windows software. The list on the right is the rule of thumb: run the least you can; code before containers, containers before clusters, and a virtual machine only for what needs one. Next, a single door for other teams.

Other teams want headroom too: the trade finance portal, the credit officers' tools, a nightly script in operations. Each could call the A P I directly, and each would need its own rules. Instead they all come through one door, API Management, which the map now has. The policy at the top, policies slash a p i m slash exposure a p i dot x m l, runs on every request before it reaches the A P I. Validate J W T requires a bearer token from the bank's Entra I D tenant, whose audience is a p i colon slash slash exposure a p i, carrying the Exposure dot Read scope; anything else is refused with four oh one. Then rate limit by key allows sixty calls a minute per subscription, which is per team. The terminal runs tools slash a p i m check dot py, a model that reads that same policy file and plays five requests through it. No authorization header: four oh one, no token. A token for Microsoft Graph: four oh one, it is for a different audience. A token for this A P I without the scope: four oh one. Omar's dashboard, on its twelfth call this minute: two hundred, passed to the A P I. And a team's script on its sixty first call: four twenty nine, retry after the minute. The table at the bottom is what the door gives other teams. A contract: the routes, published and versioned, from templates slash modules slash a p i m dot bicep. A key each: one subscription per team, so usage is visible and can be revoked team by team. Sign in: an Entra token with the right scope. And a fair share: sixty calls a minute per team, so one script cannot starve the dealers. Next, when a group goes over its limit.

Course nine promised an alert within seconds of a breach. At fifteen thirty on the fourteenth, a two million letter of credit for Wide World Importers takes Wide World Group to ten point four against its limit of ten. The intraday job sees it and publishes a limit breached event to Event Grid. The editor shows functions slash breach alert slash function app dot p y, an Azure Function in Python. Its decorators say everything: an Event Grid trigger delivers the event, and a Service Bus output binding sends whatever the function sets to the queue breach alerts, through a connection called Service Bus that uses the function's identity, not a key. The function's body is one line: it turns the event into the credit officer's message. All the logic is in message dot p y, so it can be run and tested without Azure. The terminal runs tools slash invoke breach dot p y, which calls that logic as the Functions host would, with the sample event. In: Woodgrove dot Risk dot Limit Breached, for groups slash G W W. Out, to the queue: for sam, the credit officer; group G W W; deal L C twenty forty four; reservation req c four one e; and the text: Wide World Group is over its limit, net ten point four against ten, one hundred and four per cent, the deal and its amount, and a request to approve the excess or reject the deal within thirty minutes. The first table is where a function can run. Flex Consumption, this one's plan, suits bursts, joins the virtual network and is paid per run. Premium keeps instances warm for long runs. And the Dedicated plan uses spare room on an App Service plan. The list underneath is the path: the intraday job sees the breach, Event Grid carries the event, the function writes the message, and Service Bus keeps it until it is handled. Next, what handles it.

A breach needs a person's decision, and a person may not answer. That is a workflow that waits, and the editor shows it as a Durable Functions orchestrator, functions slash breach workflow slash orchestrator dot p y. It asks the officer, and at the same moment starts a thirty minute timer. It waits for whichever finishes first. If the timer fires first, there was no answer, so it escalates to the head of credit and waits for theirs. Otherwise it cancels the timer and takes the officer's answer. If the answer is reject, it compensates, in order: it releases the deal's reservation, then tells the dealer. Whatever the answer, it records the decision. The orchestrator only decides the order; each step is an activity, and the runtime keeps the workflow's state between steps, even for hours. The terminal runs tools slash walk breach dot p y, which replaces the Durable runtime with stand in answers and runs the orchestrator's own code unchanged. In the first case, the officer approves at fifteen forty two, and the decision is recorded. In the second, the officer does not answer; at sixteen hundred the timer fires, the head of credit rejects at sixteen oh eight, the reservation is released, the dealer is told, and the decision is recorded. The table on the right compares the two ways Azure builds this. Logic Apps uses a designer and ready made connectors for email and Teams, and is tested by running it. Durable Functions is Python, uses the platform's own code, and is unit tested, which is why the platform chose it. The list underneath is compensation: a rejected excess releases the reservation, then tells the dealer, every decision is recorded, and a step is undone by another step, logged, never by deleting history.
